Day 6 — AWS Organizations -1

In real-time, most of the projects are run with multiple accounts to manage the security and isolation of workloads and shared responsibility management. And in most cases, it will be at the organizational-level account.

Why multi-accounts or OU? A single AWS account handle real enterprise needs.

An AWS account is the strongest security and blast-radius boundary in AWS.

We use  for:

  • 🧩 Independent quotas & limits
  • (stronger than IAM)

“In AWS, a management account is first created, then AWS Organizations is enabled. AWS Control Tower is built on top of Organizations and automatically creates and manages Organizational Units, guardrails, and accounts through Account Factory.”

But for the AWS practice, we can go with AWS free tier creation and use the free credits

Be cautious to avoid unexpected charges by adhering to the Free Tier limits and checking service-specific terms and usage guidelines.

AWS Management Account/Free tier creation

Step 1: Go to the AWS Homepage

Head over to AWS’s official website and click on the “Create an AWS Account” button at the top right corner of the page.

Step 2: Create Your AWS Account

Provide your contact information and agree to the AWS Customer Agreement. Click on “Verify email address.”

Enter the verification code

Step 3: Create Your AWS Account: Enter root credentials and click on “Continue (step 1 of 5)”

Provide contact information:

Step 4: Payment Information AWS requires a credit or debit card to verify your identity and prevent misuse of the Free Tier.

Don’t worry; you won’t be charged unless you explicitly use services beyond the Free Tier limits.

Step 5: Phone Verification Enter your phone number to receive a verification code. Once received, input the code and click on “Verify code and continue.”

Congratulations! Your AWS account is now created. You can sign in to the AWS Management Console to start exploring the Free Tier services.

How Accounts Are Created (Real World)

  • Root (management) account creates child accounts
  • Child accounts trust the management account
  • No resource sharing by default

AWS Organizations (The Control Plane)

A service to centrally manage multiple AWS accounts.

· Centralized billing (Consolidated Billing)

· Service Control Policies (SCPs)

· Delegated administration

There are two ways to create the OU-Multi-account setup:

1. Enterprise Setup — Using AWS Control Tower

2. Manual setup — Enabling the AWS Organizations

· As part of multi-account or real-time standards or AWS recommendations, we have to isolate workloads on different OU levels or service levels

· Along with that, we need to implement governance. The governance can be SCP, tag policies, SSO, Guard trail, Cloud trail, and other features

First, we will discuss a standard Organizational Structure, then we will try to create an AWS Multi-Account setup using a manual way, and understand the service AWS Control Tower, and how easy to setup same.

Organization Structure (Standard)

Let’s walk this exactly like a real enterprise setup, starting from your and ending at a production-ready multi-account landing zone.

You Created a Free-Tier AWS Account 👉 This account will become your Management (Root) Account. 👉 This structure is SAP-approved

│ ├── Log Archive Account

│ └── Audit / Security Tooling Account

│ └── Networking / CI-CD / AD

Organizational Units (OU) — Governance Layer

Organizational Units are logical groupings of AWS accounts within AWS Organizations that enterprises to apply governance, security, and compliance policies at scale.

Important Rule — Policies applied to an OU apply to ALL accounts under it. An OU can have multiple sub-OU’s

Different rules for Dev vs Prod, Stronger restrictions for Prod,Easier compliance enforcement

Pre-requests, before going on multi-account setup:

STEP 1️⃣ Secure the Management Account (MANDATORY FIRST)

Before anything else, do this .

  • Remove root access keys (if any)
  • Store root credentials securely
  • Use root only for billing & org-level tasks

STEP 2️⃣ : Decide the Governance Path (Decision Point)

At this point, you choose of the following:

✅ Recommended (Enterprise / SAP / Real World) — 👉 Use AWS Control Tower

⚠️ Alternative (Small / Learning Only) 👉 Manual AWS Organizations + OUs + SCPs

items.title: Building a scalable code modernization solution with AWS Transform custom
items.author: Dinesh Prabakaran
items.content:
Software maintenance and modernization is a critical challenge for enterprises managing hundreds or thousands of repositories. Whether upgrading Java versions, migrating to new AWS SDKs, or modernizing frameworks, the scale of transformation work can be overwhelming. AWS Transform custom uses agentic AI to perform large-scale modernization of software, code, libraries, and frameworks to reduce technical debt. It handles diverse scenarios including language version upgrades, API and service migrations, framework upgrades and migrations, code refactoring, and organization-specific transformations. Through continual learning, the agent improves from every execution and developer feedback, delivering high-quality, repeatable transformations without requiring specialized automation expertise.

Organizations need to run transformations using AWS Transform custom concurrently across their entire code estate to meet aggressive modernization timelines and compliance deadlines. Running it at enterprise scale requires a solution to process repositories in parallel, in a controlled remote cloud environment, manage credentials securely, and provide visibility into transformation progress. Today, we’re introducing an open-source solution that brings production-grade scalability, reliability, and monitoring to AWS Transform custom. This infrastructure enables you to run transformations on thousands of repositories in parallel using AWS Batch and AWS Fargate, with REST API access for programmatic control and comprehensive Amazon CloudWatch monitoring.

Requirements for Enterprise-Scale Code Modernization

AWS Transform custom provides powerful AI-driven code transformation capabilities through its CLI. To effectively scale transformations across enterprise codebases, organizations need:

Ability to run transformations on 1000+ repositories concurrently rather than one-by-one: Dedicated compute resources for long-running transformations beyond developers’ laptops: REST API for programmatic orchestration and seamless integration with CI/CD pipelines: Centralized visibility into transformation progress and status across multiple repositories: Automatic retries, secure credential management, and built-in fault tolerance

The Solution: Batch Infrastructure with REST API

This solution provides complete, production-ready infrastructure that addresses these challenges:

  • Scalable Batch Processing Run transformations on thousands of repositories in parallel using AWS Batch with Fargate. The default configuration (256 max vCPUs, 2 vCPUs per job) supports up to 128 concurrent jobs, with automatic queuing and resource management. The compute environment scales based on your needs and Fargate service quotas.
  • REST API for Programmatic Access Seven API endpoints provide complete job lifecycle management, enabling you to submit single jobs or bulk batches of thousands in one request. The API offers real-time status tracking and progress monitoring, with Amazon Identity and access Management (IAM) authentication ensuring secure access to transformation operations.
  • The solution includes a container supporting Java (8, 11, 17, 21), Python (3.8-3.13), and Node.js (16-24) with all build tools pre-installed, including Maven, Gradle, npm, and yarn. The AWS Transform CLI and AWS CLI v2 are bundled in. The container is fully extensible for custom requirements—you can add your own libraries, languages, or tools by customizing the Dockerfile to meet their specific needs
  • Enterprise-Grade Reliability Automatic IAM credential management eliminates long-lived keys, with credentials auto-refreshing every 45 minutes for jobs up to 12 hours. The system includes automatic retries for transient failures (default: 3 attempts), with configurable timeout and retry settings to match your transformation complexity.
  • A CloudWatch dashboard provides job tracking with success and failure rates, trends over time, and API and Lambda health metrics. Real-time log streaming enables you to monitor transformation progress and quickly diagnose issues.

The solution uses a serverless architecture built on AWS managed services:

  • REST API with IAM authentication
  • Job orchestration, status tracking, bulk submission
  • Job queue and compute environment management
  • Serverless container execution (no EC2 to manage)
  • Source code input and transformation results output
  • Logs, metrics, and operational dashboard

Before deploying, ensure you have:

  • with appropriate IAM permissions (ECR, S3, IAM, Batch, Lambda, API Gateway, CloudWatch)
  • configured with credentials or AWS SSO login
  • for cloning the repository

Option 1: CDK Deployment (Recommended)

Step 1: Clone the Repository

git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/aws-transform-custom-samples.git

cd aws-transform-custom-samples/scaled-execution-containers

Step 2: Set Environment Variables

export AWS_ACCOUNT_ID=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)
export CDK_DEFAULT_ACCOUNT=$AWS_ACCOUNT_ID
export CDK_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1

Step 3: Verify prerequisites

This checks that Docker is installed and running, AWS CLI v2 is configured with credentials, Git is available, and your AWS account has the required VPC and public subnets.

cd deployment
chmod +x *.sh
./check-prereqs.sh

Step 4: Set up IAM Permissions (Optional, but recommended)

Generate a least-privilege IAM policy instead of using broad permissions:

./generate-custom-policy.sh

This creates with minimum permissions scoped to your specific resources.

Create and attach the policy:

aws iam create-policy \
  --policy-name ATXCustomDeploymentPolicy \
  --policy-document file://iam-custom-policy.json

aws iam attach-user-policy \
  --user-name YOUR_USERNAME \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text):policy/ATXCustomDeploymentPolicy

If you have administrator access, you can skip this step and proceed directly to deployment.

Step 5: Deploy with CDK (One Command Does Everything!)

cd ../cdk
chmod +x *.sh
./deploy.sh

20-25 minutes (all resources)

What CDK Does Automatically:

  1. Builds Docker image from Dockerfile
  2. Creates all AWS resources
  • ECR repository with Docker image
  • S3 buckets (output, source)
  • IAM roles with least-privilege
  • AWS Batch infrastructure (Fargate)
  • CloudWatch logs and dashboard

See cdk/README.md for detailed instructions and configuration options.

Step 6: Get Your API Endpoint

After deployment completes, retrieve the API endpoint URL:

export API_ENDPOINT=$(aws cloudformation describe-stacks \
  --stack-name AtxApiStack \
  --query 'Stacks[0].Outputs[?OutputKey==`ApiEndpoint`].OutputValue' \
  --output text)

echo "API Endpoint: $API_ENDPOINT"

This endpoint is used in all subsequent API calls.

Option 2: Bash Scripts (Alternative)

If you prefer manual control over each deployment step or need to customize individual components, use the bash script deployment. See deployment/README.md for the complete 3-step process with detailed explanations of what each script deploys.

Run cd ../test && ./test-apis.sh to validate all API endpoints (MCP, transformations, bulk jobs, campaigns).

Submit a Python version upgrade transformation:

cd ..
python3 utilities/invoke-api.py \
  --endpoint "$API_ENDPOINT" \
  --path "/jobs" \
  --data '{
    "source": "https://github.com/venuvasu/todoapilambda",
    "command": "atx custom def exec -n AWS/python-version-upgrade -p /source/todoapilambda -c noop --configuration \"validationCommands=pytest,additionalPlanContext=The target Python version to upgrade to is Python 3.13. Python 3.13 is already installed at /usr/bin/python3.13\" -x -t"
  }'

This API call triggers a Python version upgrade transformation on the public git repository. The transformation uses the AWS Managed transformation to upgrade from the current Python version to Python 3.13. The parameter specifies additional validation command to be run and plan context to specifies the location of python 3.13 installation in the container and the target version. The flag is for non-interactive mode of the transformation , and flag is to trust all tools for this transformation.

API returns a job ID for tracking. Job names are auto-generated from the source repository and transformation type.

See api/README.md for complete API documentation with examples for Java, Node.js, and other transformations.

Transform multiple repositories in a single API call:

python3 utilities/invoke-api.py \
  --endpoint "$API_ENDPOINT" \
  --path "/jobs/batch" \
  --data '{
    "batchName": "codebase-analysis-2025",
    "jobs": [
      {"source": "https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-petclinic", "command": "atx custom def exec -n AWS/early-access-comprehensive-codebase-analysis -p /source/spring-petclinic -x -t"},
      {"source": "https://github.com/venuvasu/todoapilambda", "command": "atx custom def exec -n AWS/early-access-comprehensive-codebase-analysis -p /source/todoapilambda -x -t"},
      {"source": "https://github.com/venuvasu/toapilambdanode16", "command": "atx custom def exec -n AWS/early-access-comprehensive-codebase-analysis -p /source/toapilambdanode16 -x -t"}
    ]
  }'

This API call triggers a deep static analysis of the codebase to generate hierarchical, cross-referenced documentation for three open source repositories in parallel. The transformation uses the AWS Managed transformation to generate behavioral analysis, architectural documentation, and business intelligence extraction to create a comprehensive knowledge base organized for maximum usability and navigation.

The API submits these jobs in a async manner. i.e the API returns a batch id upon submitting these jobs to AWS Batch. Then you can monitor the progress as specified below.

See api/README.md for status checking, MCP configuration, and other API endpoints.

python3 utilities/invoke-api.py \
  --endpoint "$API_ENDPOINT" \
  --method GET \
  --path "/jobs/batch/BATCH_ID"

Response shows real-time progress:

{
  "status": "RUNNING",
  "progress": 45.5,
  "totalJobs": 1000,
  "statusCounts": {
    "RUNNING": 195,
    "SUCCEEDED": 432,
    "FAILED": 23
  }
}

After a job completes, the results are stored in your S3 output bucket.

Results are organized by job name and conversation ID:

s3://atx-custom-output-{account-id}/
└── transformations/
    └── {job-name}/                           # e.g., guava-early-access-comprehensive-codebase-analysis
        └── {timestamp}{conversation-id}/     # e.g., 20251227_051626_8f344f5f
            ├── code/                         # Full source code + transformed changes
            └── logs/                         # Execution logs and artifacts
                └── custom/
                    └── {timestamp}{conversation-id}/
                        └── artifacts/
                            └── validation_summary.md

AWS Transform CLI generates a validation summary showing all changes made:

s3://atx-custom-output-{account-id}/transformations/{job-name}/{timestamp}{conversation-id}/logs/custom/{timestamp}{conversation-id}/artifacts/validation_summary.md
  • Summary of all code changes
  • Files modified, added, or deleted
  • Transformation statistics
# Download all results for a specific job
aws s3 sync s3://atx-custom-output-{account-id}/transformations/{job-name}/{timestamp}{conversation-id}/ ./local-results/

# Download just the validation summary
aws s3 cp s3://atx-custom-output-{account-id}/transformations/{job-name}/{timestamp}{conversation-id}/logs/custom/{timestamp}{conversation-id}/artifacts/validation_summary.md ./

# Download transformed code only
aws s3 sync s3://atx-custom-output-{account-id}/transformations/{job-name}/{timestamp}{conversation-id}/code/ ./transformed-code/

Monitoring and Observability

The solution includes a CloudWatch dashboard with operational metrics:

  • Completion rate with hourly trends (completed vs failed)
  • Recent jobs table showing job name, timestamp, last message, and log stream
  • Real-time visibility into job execution
  • API Gateway request counts and error rates
  • Lambda invocation metrics per function
  • Performance monitoring (duration by function)

All logs are centralized in CloudWatch Logs () with real-time streaming.

aws logs tail /aws/batch/atx-transform --follow --region us-east-1

Or use the included utility:

python3 utilities/tail-logs.py JOB_ID --region us-east-1

View in AWS Console: CloudWatch → Log Groups →

Model Context Protocol (MCP) Integration

AWS Transform custom supports Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers to extend the AI agent with additional tools. Configure MCP servers via API:

python3 utilities/invoke-api.py \
  --endpoint "$API_ENDPOINT" \
  --path "/mcp-config" \
  --data '{
    "mcpConfig": {
      "mcpServers": {
        "github": {"command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github"]},
        "fetch": {"command": "uvx", "args": ["mcp-server-fetch"]}
      }
    }
  }'

The configuration is stored in S3 and automatically available to all transformations. Test with to list configured servers.

See api/README.md for status checking, MCP configuration, and other API endpoints.

Customization for Private Repositories

You may need to access private repositories and artifact registries. Extend the base container to add credentials:

To access your private Git repositories or artifact registries during transformations:

  1. AWS Secrets Manager (RECOMMENDED) – Credentials fetched at runtime, never stored in image
  2. Hardcode in Dockerfile (NOT RECOMMENDED) – For testing only
  1. Uncomment placeholders in (Secrets Manager) or (hardcoded)
  2. Redeploy container (see below)

Redeploying after customization:

CDK automatically detects Dockerfile changes and rebuilds. If changes aren’t detected, force rebuild:

cd cdk && ./deploy.sh —force
cd deployment
./1-build-and-push.sh --rebuild
./2-deploy-infrastructure.sh

The infrastructure will use your custom container with private repository access. You can also customize the container to add support for additional language versions or entirely new languages based on their specific requirements.

For automated PR creation and pushing changes back to remote repositories after transformation, you have two options: (1) extend with git commands using your private credentials (see commented placeholder in the script), or (2) use a custom Transformation definition with MCP configured to connect to GitHub/GitLab for more sophisticated PR workflows.

Central platform teams can create campaigns through the AWS Transform web interface to manage enterprise-wide migration and modernization projects. For instance, to upgrade all repositories from Java 8 to Java 21, teams create a campaign with the Java upgrade transformation definition and target repository list. As developers execute transformations, repositories automatically register with the campaign, enabling you to track progress and monitor across your organization.

  1. Create a Workspace and Create a Job
  2. In the chat, specify the type of the job . For example , “I would like comprehensive code analysis on multiple repos”
  3. Based on your request, AWS Transform will display the list of transformation that matches the criteria, in this case “AWS/early-access-comprehensive-codebase-analysis (Early Access)”
  4. Once you confirm the transformation, AWS Transform will create a campaign and a command to execute for the transformation. You can just copy that command and execute via the API as described below replacing the repo details.
atx custom def exec \
--code-repository-path <path-to-repo> \
--non-interactive \
--trust-all-tools \
--campaign 0d0c7e9f-5cb2-4569-8c81-7878def8e49e \
--repo-name <repo-name> \
--add-repo

Executing the Transformation in a Campaign

python3 utilities/invoke-api.py \
  --endpoint "$API_ENDPOINT" \
  --path "/jobs" \
  --data '{
    "source": "https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-petclinic",
    "command": "atx custom def exec --code-repository-path /source/spring-petclinic --non-interactive --trust-all-tools --campaign 0d0c7e9f-5cb2-4569-8c81-7878def8e49e --repo-name spring-petclinic --add-repo"
  }'

Once this transformation Job is successful, you can view the results and dashboard in Web application as well.

To remove all deployed resources:

CDK Cleanup (Recommended)

Bash Scripts Cleanup (Alternate)

cd deployment ./cleanup.sh
  • AWS Batch resources (compute environment, job queue, job definitions)
  • Lambda functions and API Gateway
  • S3 buckets (after emptying)
  • CloudWatch logs and dashboard

Enterprise software modernization requires infrastructure that can operate at scale with reliability and observability. This solution provides a production-ready platform for running AWS Transform custom transformations on thousands of repositories concurrently.

By combining AWS Batch’s scalability, Fargate’s serverless compute, and a REST API for programmatic access, you can:

  • Accelerate modernization initiatives
  • Reduce manual effort and human error
  • Gain visibility into transformation progress
  • Integrate with existing DevOps workflows

The code repository is open-source, fully automated, and ready for you to deploy in your AWS account today.

KodeKloud AWS Challenge — Day 40: Troubleshooting EC2 Internet Access in a Public VPC

A real-world troubleshooting walkthrough focused on fixing EC2 internet access issues caused by VPC misconfiguration — not security groups.

Day 40 of the KodeKloud AWS Challenge was not about resources.It was about debugging a broken architecture — a far more realistic DevOps skill.

The Nautilus Development Team deployed a web application on an EC2 instance running Nginx.Security groups were correctly configured to allow HTTP (port 80), yet the application was not accessible from the internet.

When security groups are correct and traffic still fails, the problem is almost always  — not instance-level.

Problem Statement (What Was Broken)

  • nautilus-vpc (Public VPC)
  • nautilus-ec2
  • nautilus-sg
  • Application accessible from the internet
  • Application unreachable

Security groups were already validated.So the investigation moved .

Concept Explanation: What Makes a VPC “Public”?

In Amazon Web Services, a VPC is .

For an EC2 instance to be reachable from the internet, all of the following must be true:

  1. Subnet has a route to an
  2. Internet Gateway is
  • 0.0.0.0/0 → Internet Gateway

4. EC2 instance has a

5. Security group allows inbound traffic

Miss of these, and traffic dies silently.

Architecture Overview (Correct Design)

  • User sends HTTP request from the internet
  • Request reaches the Internet Gateway
  • Route table forwards traffic to the public subnet
  • EC2 instance receives traffic on port 80
  • Nginx serves the response

If traffic never reaches the EC2 instance, .

Step-by-Step Troubleshooting (How It Was Fixed)

1️⃣ Verified Internet Gateway Attachment

  • An  existed
  • The IGW was not to the VPC
  • IGW attached to nautilus-vpc

Without an IGW, no internet traffic can enter or leave the VPC.

2️⃣ Inspected Route Tables

  • Identified the route table associated with the
  • Verified the presence of this route:
Destination: 0.0.0.0/0Target: Internet Gateway

This route was present but blackhole state:

✅ Corrected the default route to the Internet Gateway.

This step alone often fixes “EC2 not accessible” issues.

3️⃣ Confirmed Subnet Association

  • Ensured nautilus-ec2 was launched in the
  • Verified that the subnet was associated with the updated route table

A correct route table attached to the is still a failure.

4️⃣ Verified Public IP Assignment

  • Public IPv4 address was assigned

No public IP = no return path to the internet.

  • Confirmed Nginx was running
  • Accessed the EC2 instance using:
  • Application loaded successfully
  • Internet Gateway functional
  • Security groups already correct

Troubleshooting Checklist (Reusable)

When EC2 is unreachable from the internet, check in this order:

  1. Internet Gateway attached to VPC
  2. Route table has 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW
  3. Subnet association is correct
  4. Security group allows traffic
  5. Nginx / application is running

90% of the time, the issue is #2.

  • Security groups don’t create internet access
  • “Public VPC” is a design, not a checkbox
  • Routing issues fail silently
  • Debug networking before blaming applications
  • Production outages often look like this

This is real DevOps work.

Day 40 reinforced a critical lesson:

If security groups are correct, the problem is almost always routing.

By fixing the VPC configuration — specifically the Internet Gateway and route table — the Nautilus DevOps Team restored public access to the EC2-hosted application without touching the instance itself.

Understanding matters more than memorizing service options.

If you’re learning AWS or DevOps through real troubleshooting scenarios, follow the journey.Building is easy. Debugging is where engineers are made.

items.title: Build Your First CI/CD Pipeline in Azure DevOps
items.author: Sailab Banik
items.content:
Are you a developer working on a project and want to set up a basic CI/CD pipeline with Azure DevOps? Then this article is for you.

Note: There are several ways to build a CI/CD pipeline, but in this article, we will see how to design a basic one for beginners.

Azure DevOps is a Microsoft product (SaaS application) that provides the entire software development lifecycle (SDLC).

The main components of it are as follows,

  • Works on an agile system of planning and working across teams.
  • A version control environment with git support.
  • The CI/CD service that works with multiple languages and platforms to automate builds and deployments.
  • Provides testing tools to ensure quality.
  • Enables developers to share Maven, npm, NuGet, and Python package feeds from public and private sources.

In this article, we will focus only on the Repos and Pipelines tools.

What is a CI/CD Pipeline?

CI/CD is an acronym for Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment, which basically automates the software development process. As the name suggests, it has two parts,

Automates builds and tests for the code that is pushed to the repository.

Deploys the code automatically to the production environment.

The Pipelines feature in Azure DevOps helps us to continuously integrate and deploy our code in the production environment.

Now that we know what Azure DevOps is and what it means by a CI/CD pipeline, let’s perform this operation with a React application, where in the CI part, we will create a build of it, and in the CD part, we will see how to deploy the build to the remote machine as an artifact.

Permission Required for CI/CD

There are certain permissions required to create and run a CI/CD pipeline. These permissions are typically split across project-level and organization-level scopes.

The role provides access to contribute to the project. This generally includes:

  • Read and write access to repositories.
  • Ability to create and modify CI/CD pipelines
  • Permission to queue and monitor pipeline runs

In most cases, Contributor access is sufficient to author and manage CI/CD pipelines, assuming the required infrastructure permissions are already in place.

Agent pools are organization-level resources. These are the logical groupings of the agents, and an agent is nothing but the process that we are going to run on our server machine.

To create a self-hosted agent pool, a user must have:

  • The Organization Administrator role, or
  • Explicit Create / Manage Agent Pools permission at the organization level

In practice, Organization Administrators or a central DevOps/platform team usually manage agent pools. Project teams typically consume an existing pool rather than creating their own.

To run pipelines on a , the user must have permission on the pool itself.

You can verify this by navigating to:

Organization Settings → Agent Pools → <Your Agent Pool> → Security

The required permissions are:

  •  — to see the agent pool
  •  — to execute pipelines on the pool

These permissions can be assigned directly to users or groups. If access is missing, you can request the organization administrator to delegate the required authorization.

Note: Some Permissions may differ from org-to-org settings.

Repository in Azure DevOps

Click on the Repos Section, then click on the plus icon, then create a repository if not exist in your Azure DevOps.

Once created, you can clone or take a remote of your local working directory to get the files.

Once done, your Azure repository should look like the one below.

Set Up Continuous Integration

To set up continuous integration on Azure DevOps, we need to create a build pipeline.

There are two ways of doing it,

  • Click on the button from your repository.
  • Or go to the Pipelines section and click on the  button.

If you choose the second option, click in the tab, then choose the repository in the tab.

Now, in the tab, Azure will automatically detect the language and provide you with some predefined templates.

You can select the template as per the use case, or you can start with a basic Starter Pipeline.

In this case, I will go with template, which will provide me with the base YAML file for a React Project.

In the Review section, we can modify the pipeline as per our requirements, including test cases and other specifications. Once done, we can click on the  button.

And, wolla, your base Continuous Integration Pipeline is running. Whenever you make a change in your specified branch (main in our case), it will trigger this pipeline and create a build.

You can see the results of this by clicking on the Pipeline name in the Pipelines section. You can view the logs by clicking on the jobs.

Now that we know how to set up and run the CI pipeline, let’s dive into the deployment pipeline.

Continuous Deployment Pipeline

In this section, we will go step by step to deploy our React application build to a dedicated system.

Creating Artifact in the Build Pipeline

In our previous setup, we were creating the build using Azure Pipelines, but not storing it anywhere. To deploy the build, we need to create an artifact and publish it as an artifact.

An artifact in Azure Pipelines is the deployable output generated by build or CI jobs, such as compiled binaries, executable files, or packaged code (e.g., ZIP, JAR, WAR files). These files are stored and published to be consumed by later stages (e.g., testing or deployment) to ensure consistent, traceable, and reusable results.

Click on your Pipeline and go to Edit, and add the following lines of code to publish the build as an artifact.

- task: PublishBuildArtifacts@1  inputs:    ArtifactName: 'dist'
    publishLocation: 'Container'

Now, when the pipeline run is completed, it will publish an artifact that we will be able to use in our deploy/release pipeline.

In the above image, you can see that 1 published is indicating that the artifact is created and stored and on clicking on it, you can see your build files inside it.

In Azure Terminologies, CI pipeline is called Build Pipelines, and CD pipelines are called Release Pipelines.

Now, to deploy continuously in your dedicated system, go to the Agent Pools and click on your agent.

Now, click on and follow the instructions to download and set up the agent based on your platform.

In the process of config, it will ask for PAT (Personal Access Token), which you can generate in the user-settings section on the top right corner.

You need to generate the token with a few sets of permissions,

  • Agent Pools (Read and Manage)

When you’re done with your setup and hit the command it will start running the agent in your system, and you can see the machine details in your Agent Pools’ section. The machine name will appear with an online flag.

Deploy Artifact using Agent.

Now that we have our artifact and the agent setup is completed, let’s move into the last part of the deployment.

Go to Section in Azure DevOps and create a new release pipeline.

In this section, you can select any template as per your use case, or choose the Empty Job.

Now, add the artifact in the Add Artifact section, as shown inthe following image,

Now, click on the of the artifact and enable the Continuous Deployment Trigger.

Now, click on the of the Deploy to Machine stage and select your Agent Pool from this section.

In this section, on clicking on the plus (+) icon, you can create different tasks for your agent based on your use case.

Once done, save the pipeline and click on the Create Release button. And with that, your agent will start running. You can see the logs by clicking on logs.

Now, when the pipeline run is completed, you can see your build files inside your machine’s

C:\agent\_work\r1\a\<your_CI_Pipeline_Name>/dist folder.

Now, you can take this build and move it to your container or server. You can achieve this through automation in the release pipeline agent section, by clicking on the plus icon, as mentioned earlier.

And with that, our end-to-end CI/CD pipeline is ready to run and deploy your code continuously on your production environment.

I hope you can now create your first CI/CD pipeline in Azure DevOps. If this article adds value, give a clap and follow me for more such content. Comment down your thoughts in the comments.

items.title: Day 5 AWS Shared Responsibility Model andAWS Well-Architected Framework (5 Pillars)
items.author: Sai
items.content:
AWS Shared Responsibility Model

Security and compliance are shared between AWS and the customer.

Amazon Web Services secures the cloud You (customer) secure what’s in the cloud

· This shared model can help relieve the customer’s operational burden as AWS operates, manages, and controls the components from the host operating system and virtualization layer down to the physical security of the facilities in which the service operates.

· The customer assumes responsibility and management of the guest operating system (including updates and security patches), other associated application software, as well as the configuration of the AWS-provided security group firewall.

Responsibility Changes by Service Type

1️⃣ AWS Responsibility (Security the Cloud)

· Hardware (servers, storage, network)

· Physical access control

· Global infrastructure (Regions, AZs)

· Underlying virtualization layer

Customers never touch physical infrastructure.

2️⃣ Customer Responsibility (Security the Cloud)

  • IAM users, roles, permissions

“My S3 data got leaked, AWS is responsible”;

AWS secured the S3 service, You misconfigured public access

❌ “AWS is responsible for data encryption by default”✅ You must enable encryption

“AWS manages IAM policies” ✅

“Using managed services removes all security responsibility” ✅ Responsibility reduces, never disappears

🏛️ AWS Well-Architected Framework (5 Pillars)

A set of best practices and design principles to build secure, reliable, scalable, high-performing, and cost-efficient systems in AWS.

  1. Focuses on running and monitoring systems and continually improving processes and procedures to deliver business value.
  2. Protecting information, systems, and assets to manage security risk and leveraging cloud technologies for better protection.
  3. Ensuring a workload performs its intended function correctly and consistently and can recover from infrastructure or service disruptions.
  4. Using computing resources efficiently to meet system requirements and maintaining efficiency as demand changes.
  5. Avoiding unnecessary costs, running systems at the lowest price point, and delivering business value.
  6. Minimizing the environmental impact of running cloud workloads, considering long-term environmental, economic, and societal factors.

What is High Availability? Designing systems to continue operating without interruption when components fail.

  • Same AWS Region with Multiple Availability Zones
  • is about
  • EC2 instance crash in one AZ, still transactions can go on another EC2 instance of another AZ.
  • AZ power/network failure, another AZ of same region.
  • Application process crash, another EC2 instance can help.
  • Load spike, another EC2 can take load.
  • Large-scale natural disasters

HA Core Design Principles

  1. No single point of failure

· Auto Scaling Group (Multi-AZ)

· Stateless EC2 / containers

· Aurora (6 copies across 3 AZs)

· DynamoDB (multi-AZ by default)

· EBS ❌ (AZ-bound → NOT HA alone)

User -> ALB (Multi-AZ) -> EC2 (ASG in AZ-A & AZ-B) -> RDS Multi-AZ

👉 If AZ-A fails → traffic shifts to AZ-B automatically, No downtime (or seconds)

What is Disaster Recovery?

The ability to restore systems and data after a major failure or disaster. is about recovering after disaster

    • Compliance-mandated shutdown

    Key DR Metrics (SAP MUST)

    🕒 RTO (Recovery Time Objective): Maximum acceptable

    📉 RPO (Recovery Point Objective): Maximum acceptable

    • RTO = 15 minutes — App must be back in 15 min
    • RPO = 5 minutes — You can lose max 5 min of data
    • Backups in secondary region
    • Restore infra + data on disaster
    • S3 Cross-Region Replication

    Lowest cost and non-critical workloads

    • Core infra always running
    • Minimal EC2 + DB replication

    Moderate RTO/RPO and Balanced cost

    • Full system running at low scale
    • Scale instantly on disaster

      Business-critical apps

      • Traffic routed dynamically
      • Route 53 latency/failover routing

      Zero downtime requirement and Mission-critical systems

      AWS EXAM DECISION FLOW (VERY IMPORTANT)

      Does the problem mention AZ failure? → HA

      Does it mention region failure or disaster? → DR

      Does it say lowest cost? → Backup / Pilot Light

      Does it say zero downtime? → Active-Active

      INTERVIEW-READY ANSWER (PERFECT)

      “High Availability focuses on minimizing downtime within a region using multi-AZ designs, while Disaster Recovery focuses on restoring systems after regional disasters using multi-region strategies defined by RTO and RPO objectives.”

      Does the multi-region strategy setup not recognize as HA?

      High Availability focuses on handling frequent, small-scale failures with automatic, near-instant recovery, which is best achieved inside a single region using multiple Availability Zones. Multi-region introduces latency, data consistency, cost, and operational complexity, so it is classified as Disaster Recovery, not High Availability.

items.title: Ultimate Guide to Securing Your Ubuntu Servers: Cloud Firewall, UFW, and Internal Network Hardening
items.author: Muneeb Islam
items.content:
Securing your server is no longer optional — it’s critical, especially when hosting Node.js, React.js, Next.js, or PHP applications in production. In this guide, we’ll walk you through seven key security layers, combining cloud-level firewalls, OS-level firewalls, port restrictions, IP whitelisting, outbound traffic control, and private networking to build a robust defense-in-depth architecture.

1. Cloud Firewall — The First Line of Defense

Before traffic even reaches your server, a filters it. Think of it as the first checkpoint where only legitimate traffic is allowed.

  • Navigate: Dashboard → Networking → Firewalls → Create
  • ServicePortSourceSSH22Your public IP (/32)HTTP800.0.0.0/0HTTPS4430.0.0.0/0
  • Outbound rules typically allow all TCP, UDP, ICMP (needed for updates, DNS, API calls)
  • Attach the firewall to your droplets
  • EC2 → Security Groups → Create / Attach
  • Inbound rules same as above
  • Outbound rules default to allow all
  • Security Groups are , meaning response traffic is automatically allowed

Never open SSH (22) to the world (0.0.0.0/0), and avoid exposing development ports like 3000, 8000, or database ports.

2. UFW / iptables — OS-Level Firewall

Even if cloud firewalls fail, your server should protect itself. On Ubuntu, UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall) acts as a frontend to iptables, making OS-level firewall management simple and effective.

sudo ufw default deny incomingsudo ufw default allow outgoing
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp    # SSH
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp    # HTTP
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp   # HTTPS
sudo ufw allow 587/tcp   # SMTP Submission (if email server)sudo ufw status verbose

This ensures only essential inbound traffic is allowed while outbound traffic remains open for legitimate connections.

3. Allow Only Required Ports

To minimize attack surfaces, only open the ports your server needs:

  • 22 (SSH), 80 (HTTP), 443 (HTTPS), 25/465/587 (SMTP for email), 53 (DNS), 123 (NTP)
  • 3000, 8000, 9000, 3306 (MySQL), 27017 (MongoDB), 6379 (Redis), 5432 (PostgreSQL)

If a service isn’t directly accessed by clients, keep its port closed.

4. IP Whitelisting for Admin Panels

Protect admin dashboards (/admin, /dashboard, /phpmyadmin) by allowing only trusted IPs:

location /admin {    allow 103.xxx.xxx.xxx;}
<Directory "/var/www/html/admin">    Require ip 103.xxx.xxx.xxx

This prevents bots and attackers from even reaching the login page.

5. Extra Hardening — Basic Auth (Double Lock)

Adding HTTP Basic Authentication at the server level creates a :

  1. Basic Auth popup at the browser level
  2. Application login credentials
sudo apt install apache2-utils
sudo htpasswd -c /etc/nginx/.htpasswd adminuser
location /admin {    auth_basic "Restricted Admin Area";
    auth_basic_user_file /etc/nginx/.htpasswd;
    allow 103.xxx.xxx.xxx;    deny all;
sudo nginx -tsudo systemctl reload nginx

Browser prompts for username and password before even loading the admin panel. Combined with IP whitelisting, it blocks almost all automated attacks.

6. Block Unused Outbound Traffic

Outbound traffic control prevents compromised services from calling random servers.

sudo ufw default deny outgoingsudo ufw allow out 80/tcp    # HTTP
sudo ufw allow out 443/tcp   # HTTPS
sudo ufw allow out 53/udp    # DNS
sudo ufw allow out 53/tcp
sudo ufw allow out 123/udp   # NTP
sudo ufw allow out 25/tcp    # SMTP
sudo ufw allow out 465/tcp   # SMTPS
sudo ufw allow out 587/tcp   # SMTP Submission

This ensures that only essential traffic is allowed, preventing malware or compromised apps from communicating with external attackers.

7. Separate Internal Services via Private Network

Your database and internal services should never be publicly exposed.

  • Use VPC, app connects via DB’s private IP
  • Place DB in a private subnet; app EC2 in public subnet. Security Group allows DB access only from the app server’s SG
  • Brute-force attacks blocked
  • Database invisible to the Internet
  • Strong network-level isolation
  1. Cloud Firewall / Security Group → First line of defense
  2. UFW / iptables → OS-level firewall
  3. Only required ports → Reduce attack surface
  4. IP whitelist + Basic Auth → Protect admin panels
  5. Outbound restrictions → Contain malware
  6. Private network for internal services → DB and internal services never exposed

These layers work together to ensure your server is secure from the Internet and internal misconfigurations.

items.title: Reduce Vulnerability Noise with VEX: Wiz + Docker Hardened Images
items.author: Dan Berezin Stelzer
items.content:
Open source components power most modern applications. A new generation of hardened container images can establish a more secure foundation, but even with hardened images, vulnerability scanners often return dozens or hundreds of CVEs with little prioritization. This noise slows teams down and complicates security triage. The VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange) standard addresses the problem by providing information on whether a specific vulnerability actually impacts an organization’s application stack and infrastructure.

A new integration between Docker Hardened Images (DHI) and Wiz CLI now gives security and platform teams accurate reachability insights by analyzing VEX data. Wiz worked with Docker to tune its scanners to properly ingest and parse the VEX statements included with every one of the more than 1,000 DHI images in the catalog. The integration helps users cut through vulnerability noise with scan results that deliver clear, actionable insights.

When the Wiz scanner detects a Docker Hardened Image, it pulls from the image’s VEX documents and OSV advisories to filter out false positives. For organizations already using Wiz, this means a simpler path to adopting hardened images across their container fleet. Finally, for organizations pursuing FedRAMP or other compliance certifications that specify VEX coverage, the ability of Wiz to read DHI VEX statements can accelerate compliance, reducing time to deployment and consequently time to revenue.

Integrate Docker with Wiz to:

  • Minimize false positives using VEX and OSV data
  • Identify base images and software components more accurately
  • Provide security teams with clear visibility into software bills of materials (SBOMs)
  • Reduce manual validation efforts by integrating detailed issue summaries into your remediation workflows
  • Better image quality assurance with up-to-date package metadata and SPDX snippets
  • Migrate to Docker Hardened Images with greater confidence

VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange) is a machine-readable way for software suppliers to state whether a known vulnerability actually affects a specific product. Instead of inferring risk from dependency lists alone, VEX explicitly declares whether a vulnerability is not affected, affected, fixed, or under investigation. This matters because many scanner findings are not exploitable in real products, leading to false positives, wasted effort, and obscured real risk.VEX  enables transparent, auditable vulnerability status that security tools and customers can independently verify, unlike proprietary advisory feeds that obscure context and historical risk.

  • Ensure you have access to both your Docker and Wiz organizations;
  • Confirm your are using a Docker Hardened Image
  • Ensure you have SBOM export and scan visibility enabled in Wiz.
  • Identifying Docker Hardened Images via the Integration on Wiz
  • With the integration, Wiz automatically detects Docker Hardened Images. The integration consists of two main functionalities on the Wiz dashboard. First, we will verify how many resources and organizations are using Docker Hardened Images by following these steps: 
  • You’ll be prompted to log in to your Wiz dashboard
  • Once logged in, navigate to the section on the left side bar of your dashboard
  • You’ll be redirected to the “Technology” dashboard, where Wiz detects all technologies running on customer environments. Now, look for “Docker Hardened Images” on the search bar
  • Wiz automatically detects the specific operating systems running on each container mounts and flags them as hardened images

Checking for vulnerabilities on the Wiz dashboard:

Once you’ve validated that Wiz can identify Docker Hardened Images, you will be able to check for vulnerabilities using Wiz’s security graph and Docker’s container metadata. In order to do that, follow these steps from the technologies tab:

  • Go to inventory/technologies page and filter by operating systems or search for specific technology
  • Click on the OS/technology to view metadata and resource count
  • Click to access the security graph view showing all resources running that technology
  • Add a condition to filter for CVEs detected on those resources. 
  • View all resources with their associated vulnerabilities in table or graph format

After setup, the vulnerabilities will appear according to your pre-set policies. You’ll be able to get a detailed overview on each CVE listed, including graph visualizations for dependency relationships, severity distribution, and potential exploit paths. These insights will help you prioritize remediation efforts, track resolution progress, and ensure compliance with your organization’s security standards.

Integrating Docker Hardened Images for better software supply chain visibility

The Docker-Wiz integration is more than just a checkbox in your security checklist. It provides:

  • : VEX documents and accurate base image identification eliminate guesswork, providing clear, contextual vulnerability data.
  • : Minimized false positives through OSV advisories and Docker-provided metadata ensures security teams can trust what they see.
  • : Enhanced visibility into SBOMs and technology usage empowers teams to prioritize and manage remediation effectively.
  • : Full-stack integration with Wiz surfaces vulnerabilities across all Docker environments, including hardened images and source-built components.This partnership helps DevSecOps teams move fast and remain proactive against container vulnerabilities, an essential capability for modern, lean teams managing fast-paced releases, open source risk, and complex cloud-native environments.

If you’re already using Docker Hardened Images and Wiz, you’re just a few clicks away from reducing false positives, improving SBOM visibility, and making vulnerability data more actionable.

items.title: 3 AM. Production Down. Pods Failing. These 5 kubectl Commands Saved Me $50K.
items.author: Devrim Ozcay
items.content:
The kubectl commands that separate junior engineers from seniors. No theory. Just production debugging.

The PagerDuty alert came at 3:17 AM.

“Payment service down. 500s across all endpoints. Revenue stopped.”

I rolled out of bed. Opened my laptop. Kubernetes dashboard showed red everywhere.

12 pods in CrashLoopBackOff. Memory graphs spiking. CPU throttling. Load balancer health checks failing.

I had no idea what to do.

I spent 40 minutes clicking through Kubernetes dashboards. Restarted pods randomly. Made it worse.

By 4 AM, we’d lost $50,000 in failed transactions. Payment processor started blocking our requests.

That’s when my tech lead joined the call.

He typed 5 kubectl commands. In 8 minutes, he found the issue. In 12 minutes, production was stable.

I learned more in those 12 minutes than in 6 months of Kubernetes tutorials.

Command #1: kubectl get pods -o wide — sort-by=.status.startTime

Shows pod status sorted by start time. Instantly reveals which pods are restarting repeatedly.

When 50 pods are running, you can’t tell which ones are actually broken. The Kubernetes dashboard shows “Running” for pods that are crashing every 30 seconds.

I looked at pod count. Saw “12/15 Running” and thought “most are fine.”

Those 12 “running” pods? 8 were in restart loops. They’d start, crash after 15 seconds, restart, crash again.

Kubernetes counted them as “Running” because they were running . They just wouldn’t be running in 20 seconds.

What My Tech Lead Saw Instantly:

kubectl get pods -o wide --sort-by=.status.startTime
NAME                           READY   STATUS             RESTARTS   AGE
payment-api-7d9f8c-xkp2m      0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   47         8m
payment-api-7d9f8c-mnb4k      0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   45         8m
payment-api-7d9f8c-qwe9j      0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   44         8m
payment-worker-5c8a2-zxc3v    1/1     Running            2          2m
payment-worker-5c8a2-asd7n    1/1     Running            1          2m

“See the restart counts? 47 times in 8 minutes. Something’s crashing them immediately.”

High restart count + short age = configuration issue or missing dependency.

Low restart count + recent start = probably fine.

I wasted 40 minutes looking at CPU graphs. The real issue was right there: pods couldn’t start because of a bad config.

One command would have shown me that in 10 seconds.

Command #2: kubectl describe pod <pod-name> | grep -A 10 “Events:”

Shows the last 10 Kubernetes events for a pod. The actual error messages.

Pod logs show your application errors. Kubernetes events show why Kubernetes can’t run your pod.

I ran kubectl logs payment-api-7d9f8c-xkp2m.

“How can there be no logs? It’s crashing!”

What My Tech Lead Explained:

“If the pod crashes before your application starts, there are no application logs. You need to see what Kubernetes sees.”

kubectl describe pod payment-api-7d9f8c-xkp2m | grep -A 10 "Events:"  Type     Reason     Age                   From               Message
  ----     ------     ----                  ----               -------
  Normal   Scheduled  9m                    default-scheduler  Successfully assigned default/payment-api-7d9f8c-xkp2m
  Normal   Pulled     9m                    kubelet            Successfully pulled image "payment-api:v2.4.1"
  Normal   Created    9m                    kubelet            Created container payment-api
  Normal   Started    9m                    kubelet            Started container payment-api
  Warning  BackOff    8m (x42 over 9m)      kubelet            Back-off restarting failed container
  Warning  Failed     3m (x40 over 9m)      kubelet            Error: ImagePullBackOff

“See that? ImagePullBackOff. Your deployment references an image tag that doesn't exist."

Someone deployed payment-api:v2.4.1. Docker registry only had payment-api:v2.4.0.

Typo in the deployment YAML. One character. $50K in lost revenue.

# Check what image the pod is trying to pullkubectl get pod payment-api-7d9f8c-xkp2m -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].image}'
# Output: payment-api:v2.4.1
# Check available images in registry
# (Found v2.4.0, not v2.4.1)
# Fix the deployment
kubectl set image deployment/payment-api payment-api=payment-api:v2.4.0
# Verify
kubectl rollout status deployment/payment-api

Application logs tell you what your code is doing.

Kubernetes events tell you what Kubernetes is doing with your code.

Command #3: kubectl top pods — containers

Shows real-time CPU and memory usage per container. Not what’s configured. What’s actually being used.

Your pod is “Running” but something’s wrong. Is it memory? CPU? Neither?

After fixing the image tag issue, pods started. Then immediately OOMKilled (Out of Memory).

I looked at the resource requests:

resources:  requests:  limits:

“1GB should be enough. What’s wrong?”

kubectl top pods --containers
POD                              CONTAINER      CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
payment-api-7d9f8c-xkp2m        payment-api     89m          987Mi
payment-api-7d9f8c-mnb4k        payment-api     92m          1012Mi  # OOMKilled here
payment-api-7d9f8c-qwe9j        payment-api     88m          995Mi

“Your pods are hitting the 1GB limit. They’re getting killed because they’re using more memory than you allowed.”

When pods show high memory usage close to their limit, they’re about to OOMKill.

When CPU shows throttling (in kubectl describe), pods slow down but don't crash.

Memory kills. CPU throttles.

We added a new feature that loads all active sessions into memory. In staging: 100 users. In production: 15,000 users.

Memory usage scaled linearly with active users. We never load tested with real user counts.

# Temporary fix: increase memory limitkubectl set resources deployment payment-api --limits=memory=2Gikubectl top pods --containers --watch
# Real fix: change session storage from in-memory to Redis
# (Did that the next morning)

Staging doesn’t teach you about production memory usage.

Production does. And it teaches you at 3 AM.

Command #4: kubectl logs <pod-name> — previous

Shows logs from the container before it crashed.

When a pod crashes and restarts, kubectl logs shows logs from the container. Which just started. And has no errors yet.

After increasing memory, pods still crashed occasionally. Not every time. Just… sometimes.

I’d run kubectl logs payment-api-7d9f8c-xkp2m.

Logs looked fine. Startup sequence. Health check passed. Then nothing.

“Why are the logs empty when it crashes?”

What My Tech Lead Showed Me:

# Current container logs (useless, pod just restarted)kubectl logs payment-api-7d9f8c-xkp2m
2024-02-04 03:45:12 INFO  Starting payment-api v2.4.0
2024-02-04 03:45:13 INFO  Connected to database
2024-02-04 03:45:14 INFO  Health check endpoint ready
# Previous container logs (the one that crashed)
kubectl logs payment-api-7d9f8c-xkp2m --previous
2024-02-04 03:42:10 INFO  Processing payment batch
2024-02-04 03:42:15 ERROR Failed to acquire database lock
2024-02-04 03:42:15 ERROR Deadlock detected: payments.lock_version
2024-02-04 03:42:16 FATAL Unrecoverable error, shutting down

“There. Database deadlock. Your pods are crashing because of concurrent payment processing.”

Two pods tried to process the same payment batch. Pessimistic locking. Deadlock. Crash.

Why didn’t we see this in staging? Because staging only had 1 pod. Can’t deadlock with yourself.

# Check how many replicaskubectl get deployment payment-api
# Add distributed locking (Redis)
# Add idempotency keys
# Add proper error handling instead of FATAL exit
# Verify no more crashes

The crash logs aren’t in the current container.

They’re in the previous one.

And that previous container? It’s gone. Unless you know --previous.

Command #5: kubectl get events — sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp

Shows cluster-level events sorted by time. The timeline of what Kubernetes did.

You’re debugging one pod. But the issue isn’t the pod. It’s the .

After fixing deadlocks, we were stable for 20 minutes. Then suddenly:

  • 3 pods failed to schedule

“What the hell is happening?”

kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp | tail -20
3m    Warning   Evicted              Pod    payment-api-7d9f8c-xkp2m    Node disk pressure
3m    Warning   Evicted              Pod    payment-api-7d9f8c-mnb4k    Node disk pressure
3m    Warning   Evicted              Pod    payment-worker-5c8a2-zxc3v  Node disk pressure
2m    Warning   NodeNotReady         Node   node-1                      Disk pressure detected
2m    Warning   FailedScheduling     Pod    payment-api-7d9f8c-new1     0/3 nodes available: disk pressure

“Your nodes are running out of disk space. Kubernetes is evicting pods to free up space.”

We enabled debug logging during the incident. Every request logged full JSON payloads.

15,000 requests per minute × 5KB per log = 75MB/minute.

In 40 minutes: 3GB of logs filled the node disk.

# Check disk usage on nodeskubectl describe node node-1 | grep -A 5 "Conditions:"
# Emergency: delete old logs
kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -- shrm -rf /var/log/old/*
# Proper fix: configure log rotation
# Set log retention to 1 day
# Ship logs to external storage (CloudWatch, etc.)
# Verify nodes recovered

Single pod issues? Check pod events.

Multiple pods failing? Check cluster events.

The cluster knows things your pods don’t.

Kubernetes in Production — Deployment, Scaling & Troubleshooting Pack

What I Learned at 3:17 AM

After that incident, I changed how I debug Kubernetes.

  • Restart things hoping they’d fix themselves

    The difference wasn’t skill. It was knowing which commands show which problems.

    My New Debugging Checklist:

    # 1. Which pods are actually broken?kubectl get pods -o wide --sort-by=.status.startTime
    # 2. Why can't they start?
    kubectl describe pod <pod-name> | grep -A 10 "Events:"
    # 3. Are they hitting resource limits?
    kubectl top pods --containers
    # 4. What error killed the previous container?
    kubectl logs <pod-name> --previous
    # 5. Is this a cluster-wide issue?
    kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp | tail -20

    Run these 5 commands. In order. Before doing anything else.

    They would have saved me 40 minutes and $50K.

    The Free Checklist That Changed How I Debug

    Look, I wish someone had given me this checklist before that 3 AM disaster.

    So I built it. The exact debugging workflow I use now for every production Kubernetes issue:

    • Kubernetes debugging decision tree
    • Command cheat sheet for every incident type
    • Pre-deployment validation checklist
    • Rollback procedures that actually work

    I also documented my entire production debugging workflow in:

    Because most Kubernetes issues aren’t Kubernetes issues. They’re application configuration issues that manifest in Kubernetes.

    What Seniors Know That Juniors Don’t

    After that incident, I asked my tech lead: “How did you know those commands?”

    He said: “I’ve debugged this exact issue 47 times. Different companies. Different apps. Same root causes.”

    Production failures follow patterns.

    • Image tag typos → kubectl describe pod
    • Memory issues → kubectl top pods
    • Crash loops → kubectl logs --previous
    • Node issues → kubectl get events

    The commands don’t change. The root causes don’t change. Only the company names change.

    Senior engineers aren’t smarter. They’ve just seen the same failures more times.

    And they’ve documented what works.

    The Hard Truth About Kubernetes

    Kubernetes doesn’t make your application production-ready.

    • Automatic restarts (great for crashes)
    • Load balancing (great for traffic)
    • Horizontal scaling (great for growth)

      Your application can be garbage, and Kubernetes will keep restarting that garbage forever.

      The trick isn’t learning Kubernetes.

      It’s learning what Kubernetes is telling you when your application fails.

      The Commands I Wish I’d Known

      If I could go back to 3:17 AM, I’d tell myself:

      Stop clicking dashboards. Run these 5 commands.

      They won’t prevent the incident. But they’ll cut your debugging time from 40 minutes to 8 minutes.

      And at $50K per hour of downtime?

      Those 32 minutes are worth learning these commands.

      If you’re working on real production systems, I documented everything I learned here:

      And if you’re dealing with Spring Boot + Kubernetes specifically:

      I write about production failures every week. Real incidents. Real lessons. No fluff.

      That $50K incident taught me more than any Kubernetes course. But I’d rather you learn from my mistakes than make them yourself.

      If you’ve had your own 3 AM Kubernetes disaster, I want to hear it. The patterns are real. And every failure documented is a failure prevented for someone else.

items.author: Sanjal S Eralil
items.content:
DNS Resolution in K8s :From Service Discovery to Pod Routing- Complete Flow

When I first started working with Kubernetes, one thing puzzled me: containers could magically find each other by name, regardless of where they were running or how many times they restarted. Kubernetes seemed to handle everything automatically.

But how does a frontend Pod running on Node 1 find a database Pod on Node 3 just by querying “postgres”? How does traffic actually reach the right Pod when there are dozens of replicas? And what’s really happening when we create a Service?

In this deep dive, we’ll explore:

  • How CoreDNS provides cluster-wide service discovery
  • The role of label selectors in routing traffic to Pods
  • How Services bridge the gap between names and IPs
  • What changes (and what doesn’t) with different Service types

Part 1: The Foundation — Understanding K8s Networking

The Pod Networking Challenge

In Kubernetes, Pods are . They get created, destroyed, and rescheduled constantly:

Time T0:┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ api-pod-1: 10.244.1.5  (Node 1)                │
│ api-pod-2: 10.244.2.8  (Node 2)                │
│ api-pod-3: 10.244.3.12 (Node 3)                │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Time T1: api-pod-2 crashes, gets replaced┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ api-pod-1: 10.244.1.5  (Node 1)                │
│ api-pod-4: 10.244.1.20 (Node 1) ← New IP!      │
│ api-pod-3: 10.244.3.12 (Node 3)                │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

If your frontend is configured to connect to 10.244.2.8, it breaks when that Pod is replaced. You can't hardcode Pod IPs!

Kubernetes uses a two-layer approach:

  1.  — Provide stable virtual IPs (ClusterIPs)
  2.  — Maps service names to those stable IPs

This is the foundation of service discovery in Kubernetes.

Part 2: CoreDNS — The Cluster DNS Server

CoreDNS is a flexible, plugin-based DNS server that runs as a Deployment inside your cluster. Think of it as your cluster’s internal phone book.

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐│  kube-system Namespace                                  │
│                                                          │
│  ┌─────────────┐      ┌─────────────┐                 │
│  │  CoreDNS    │      │  CoreDNS    │                 │
│  │  Pod #1     │      │  Pod #2     │                 │
│  └─────────────┘      └─────────────┘                 │
│         ↑                     ↑                         │
│         └──────────┬──────────┘                         │
│                    │                                    │
│         ┌──────────▼────────────┐                      │
│         │  kube-dns Service     │                      │
│         │  ClusterIP: 10.96.0.10│                      │
│         └──────────┬────────────┘                      │
└────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┘
                     │
      All Pods query this IP for DNS

Checking CoreDNS in Your Cluster

# View CoreDNS podskubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
# Output:NAME                       READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
coredns-74ff55c5b-7mqxj   1/1     Running   0          45d
coredns-74ff55c5b-n8lkw   1/1     Running   0          45d
# View the kube-dns Servicekubectl get svc -n kube-system kube-dns
# Output:NAME       TYPE        CLUSTER-IP   EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)         AGE
kube-dns   ClusterIP   10.96.0.10   <none>        53/UDP,53/TCP   90d

Every Pod in your cluster is automatically configured to use 10.96.0.10 for DNS queries!

Inside a Pod’s DNS Configuration

Let’s see what a Pod actually sees:

# Create a test podkubectl run test-pod --image=busybox --restart=Never -- sleep 3600
# Check its DNS configkubectl exec test-pod -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
Output:```search default.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
  1.  — All DNS queries go to CoreDNS
  2.  — Automatic completion for short names
  • default.svc.cluster.local - Services in same namespace
  • svc.cluster.local - Services in any namespace
  • cluster.local - Cluster domain

3. — Query behavior control (we’ll explore this later)

Part 3: Services — The Stable Endpoint Layer

Before DNS can work, we need something stable to resolve to. Enter: .

Creating Pods with Labels

First, let’s create some Pods. The key here is  — they’re how Services find Pods:

# api-pods.yamlapiVersion: v1metadata:  labels:
    app: api           # Label 1
    version: v1        # Label 2
    tier: backend      # Label 3
spec:  - name: api
    image: hashicorp/http-echo
    args:
    - "-text=Hello from Pod 1"
    - "-listen=:8080"    - containerPort: 8080apiVersion: v1metadata:  labels:    version: v1spec:  - name: api
    image: hashicorp/http-echo
    args:
    - "-text=Hello from Pod 2"
    - "-listen=:8080"    - containerPort: 8080apiVersion: v1metadata:  labels:    version: v1spec:  - name: api
    image: hashicorp/http-echo
    args:
    - "-text=Hello from Pod 3"
    - "-listen=:8080"    - containerPort: 8080
kubectl apply -f api-pods.yaml
# Check the podskubectl get pods -o wide
Output:```
NAME        READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   IP            NODE
api-pod-1   1/1     Running   0          10s   10.244.1.5    node-1
api-pod-2   1/1     Running   0          10s   10.244.2.8    node-2
api-pod-3   1/1     Running   0          10s   10.244.3.12   node-3

Creating a Service with Label Selectors

Now let’s create a Service that uses to find these Pods:

# api-service.yamlapiVersion: v1metadata:spec:    app: api       # Match Pods with app=api
    version: v1    # AND version=v1
  ports:    port: 80         # Service port (what clients connect to)
    targetPort: 8080 # Pod port (where traffic goes)
  type: ClusterIP
kubectl apply -f api-service.yaml
# Check the servicekubectl get svc api-service
Output:```
NAME          TYPE        CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)   AGE
api-service   ClusterIP   10.100.50.10   <none>        80/TCP    5s

Part 4: The Magic — How Label Selectors Route to Pods

When you create a Service with a selector, Kubernetes automatically creates an object with the same name:

kubectl get endpoints api-service```
Output:```
NAME          ENDPOINTS                                      AGE
api-service   10.244.1.5:8080,10.244.2.8:8080,10.244.3.12:8080   30s

Let’s look at the full object:

kubectl get endpoints api-service -o yaml
apiVersion: v1kind: Endpoints  name: api-service  # Same name as the Service!- addresses:    targetRef:      name: api-pod-1    targetRef:      name: api-pod-2    targetRef:      name: api-pod-3  - port: 8080
this is the bridge between the service and the pod

(running in kube-controller-manager) continuously:

  1. all Services with selectors
  • : “Find all Pods matching these labels”
  • : Only include  Pods
  • : Get their IP addresses
  • : Write to object
  1. watches
  2. updates rules

Tracing the process of endpoint creation

# Watch the endpoints in real-time
kubectl get endpoints api-service -w
# Delete a podkubectl delete pod api-pod-2
Back in the watch terminal, you'll see:```
NAME          ENDPOINTS                                AGE
api-service   10.244.1.5:8080,10.244.3.12:8080        1m               └── Pod 2 removed immediately!

The Endpoint Controller detected that api-pod-2 is gone and updated the Endpoints object instantly.

Testing Label Selector Matching

# See which Pods match the Service selectorkubectl get pods -l app=api,version=v1
# Output:NAME        READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
api-pod-1   1/1     Running   0          5m
api-pod-2   1/1     Running   0          5m
api-pod-3   1/1     Running   0          5m
apiVersion: v1kind: Pod  name: api-pod-v2    app: api
    version: v2      # Different version!
    tier: backend  containers:    image: hashicorp/http-echo    - "-text=Hello from v2"    ports:
kubectl apply -f api-pod-v2.yaml
# Check if it's in the endpointskubectl get endpoints api-service
Output:```
NAME          ENDPOINTS                                      AGE
api-service   10.244.1.5:8080,10.244.2.8:8080,10.244.3.12:8080   10m
Notice: The v2 Pod is NOT included! The selector requires `version: v1`.

Part 5: DNS Resolution — Putting It All Together

Now let's see how DNS resolves service names to ClusterIPs.
### The Complete DNS Resolution Flow
```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STEP 1: Application Makes Request                       │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────┐                      │
│  │  Client Pod                     │                      │
│  │  curl http://api-service        │                      │
│  └────────────┬───────────────────┘                      │
└───────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┘
                │┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STEP 2: DNS Lookup Triggered                            │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────┐                      │
│  │  /etc/resolv.conf says:        │                      │
│  │  nameserver 10.96.0.10         │                      │
│  │  search default.svc.cluster... │                      │
│  └────────────┬───────────────────┘                      │
└───────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┘
                │┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STEP 3: Apply Search Domains                            │
│  'api-service' has 1 dot (< 5)                           │
│  Try: api-service.default.svc.cluster.local ✓            │
└───────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┘                ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STEP 4: Query CoreDNS                                   │
│  DNS query to 10.96.0.10:53                              │
│  Question: IP of api-service.default.svc.cluster.local?  │
└───────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┘
                │┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STEP 5: CoreDNS Processes Request                       │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────┐                      │
│  │  1. Parse query                │                      │
│  │  2. Query Kubernetes API:      │                      │
│  │     "Get Service 'api-service' │                      │
│  │      in namespace 'default'"   │                      │
│  │  3. K8s returns ClusterIP      │                      │
│  │  4. Build DNS response         │                      │
│  └────────────┬───────────────────┘                      │
└───────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┘                ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STEP 6: DNS Response                                    │
│  Answer: api-service = 10.100.50.10                      │
│  TTL: 30 seconds                                         │
└───────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┘
                │┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STEP 7: Connect to Service ClusterIP                   │
│  Client connects to 10.100.50.10:80                      │
└───────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┘
                │┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  STEP 8: kube-proxy Routes to Pod                       │
│  iptables rules route to one of:                         │
│  - 10.244.1.5:8080  (Pod 1)                             │
│  - 10.244.2.8:8080  (Pod 2)                             │
│  - 10.244.3.12:8080 (Pod 3)                             │
│  ✅ Request succeeds!                                    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
# Test DNS from our test podkubectl exec test-pod -- nslookup api-service```Address 1: 10.96.0.10 kube-dns.kube-system.svc.cluster.localAddress 1: 10.100.50.10 api-service.default.svc.cluster.local

Perfect! DNS returned the Service's ClusterIP.

# Make an HTTP request using the service namekubectl exec test-pod -- wget -qO- http://api-service```
kubectl exec test-pod -- wget -qO- http://api-service``````

Load balancing in action! Each request hits a different Pod.

Part 6: How Traffic Actually Reaches Pods (kube-proxy)

We know DNS gives us the ClusterIP (10.100.50.10), but ClusterIP is just a - it doesn't actually exist on any network interface! So how does traffic reach the real Pods?

Answer: kube-proxy creates iptables rules that intercept traffic destined for ClusterIPs and redirects it to actual Pod IPs.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐│                                                                 │
│  CLIENT POD                                                     │
│  "I want to connect to 10.100.50.10:80"                        │
│                                                                 │
└────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘                             ▼
         Packet leaves pod with destination:
                  10.100.50.10:80                             ▼
╔═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                                                                 ║
║  NODE'S NETWORK STACK                                          ║
║  (iptables rules created by kube-proxy)                        ║
║                                                                 ║
║  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ ║
║  │ Rule: If destination = 10.100.50.10:80                    │ ║
║  │       Then randomly pick a Pod:                           │ ║
║  │                                                            │ ║
║  │       • 33% → Change to 10.244.1.5:8080                  │ ║
║  │       • 33% → Change to 10.244.2.8:8080                  │ ║
║  │       • 33% → Change to 10.244.3.12:8080                 │ ║
║  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ║
║                                                                 ║
╚═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
                             │
         Packet now has destination:
                  10.244.2.8:8080                             ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                 │
│  DESTINATION POD                                                │
│  Routed to actual Pod on Node 2                                │
│  ✅ Connection established!                                     │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Understanding Kubernetes DNS reveals the elegant simplicity behind what initially seems like magic. When you type curl http://api-service, a precisely orchestrated chain unfolds: CoreDNS resolves the name to a stable ClusterIP, label selectors connect the Service to matching Pods through Endpoints, and kube-proxy's iptables rules route traffic to a healthy Pod — all in milliseconds.

The beauty lies in the abstraction. Pods crash, scale, and move between nodes, yet your application code never changes. DNS always returns the same ClusterIP, while the Endpoint Controller quietly updates which Pods receive traffic behind the scenes.

This knowledge transforms how you debug: slow DNS? Check ndots. No endpoints? Verify label selectors. Connection refused? Inspect Pod readiness probes. You're no longer guessing — you understand the system.
