CI/CD Pipeline Best PracticesCI/CD Pipeline Best Practices for 2025: Building Resilient, Secure, and Efficient Software Delivery

Revolutionizing software delivery with modern CI/CD strategies for the cloud-native era

As we navigate through 2025, the software development landscape continues to evolve at an unprecedented pace. Organizations worldwide are racing to deliver software faster, more reliably, and more securely than ever before. At the heart of this transformation lies the Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline — the backbone of modern DevOps practices.

In this comprehensive guide, we’ll explore the essential best practices that define successful CI/CD implementations in 2025, covering everything from security-first approaches to cloud-native optimization strategies.

The Evolution of CI/CD in 2025

The CI/CD landscape has matured significantly, with organizations now prioritizing security, automation, and cloud-native technologies. Modern pipelines are no longer just about speed; they’re about building resilient, secure, and scalable delivery mechanisms that can adapt to the demands of distributed systems and microservices architectures.

Key trends shaping CI/CD in 2025 include:

  • for intelligent pipeline optimization
  • integration
  • Cloud-native and Kubernetes-first approaches
  • and observability
  • Multi-cloud and hybrid deployment strategies

1. Embrace Security-First CI/CD (DevSecOps)

Security can no longer be an afterthought in modern CI/CD pipelines. The “shift-left” approach has become the standard, integrating security checks throughout the entire development lifecycle.

Implement Automated Security Scanning

  • Integrate Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tools early in the pipeline
  • Use Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) for runtime vulnerability detection
  • Implement Software Composition Analysis (SCA) to identify vulnerable dependencies
  • Conduct Infrastructure as Code (IaC) security scans before deployment
  • Never hardcode secrets in your codebase or pipeline configurations
  • Use dedicated secrets management tools like HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or Azure Key Vault
  • Implement proper secret rotation policies
  • Ensure secrets are encrypted both in transit and at rest

Access Control and Authentication

  • Implement least-privilege access principles
  • Use multi-factor authentication for all pipeline access
  • Regularly audit and review access permissions
  • Implement role-based access control (RBAC) for different pipeline stages

2. Optimize for Cloud-Native and Kubernetes Deployment

The shift toward cloud-native architectures has fundamentally changed how we approach CI/CD. Modern pipelines must seamlessly integrate with containerization and orchestration platforms.

Cloud-Native Best Practices:

  • Build immutable container images for consistent deployments
  • Implement multi-stage Docker builds to minimize image size and attack surface
  • Use container image scanning tools to identify vulnerabilities
  • Implement proper image tagging and versioning strategies
  • Use Helm charts or Kustomize for Kubernetes deployment management
  • Implement GitOps workflows with tools like ArgoCD or Flux
  • Utilize Kubernetes-native CI/CD tools that understand cluster resources
  • Implement proper resource limits and requests for containerized workloads

Infrastructure as Code (IaC)

  • Version control all infrastructure definitions
  • Implement infrastructure testing and validation
  • Use tools like Terraform, Pulumi, or AWS CDK for infrastructure provisioning
  • Establish proper environment parity between development, staging, and production

3. Implement Comprehensive Testing Strategies

A robust testing strategy is crucial for maintaining code quality and preventing production issues. Modern CI/CD pipelines must incorporate multiple layers of testing.

Multi-Layered Testing Approach:

  • Maintain high code coverage (aim for 80%+ meaningful coverage)
  • Implement fast, isolated unit tests that run on every commit
  • Use test-driven development (TDD) practices where appropriate
  • Ensure tests are maintainable and provide clear failure messages

Integration and End-to-End Testing

  • Implement API contract testing to ensure service compatibility
  • Use tools like Cypress, Playwright, or Selenium for UI testing
  • Create realistic test data and environments
  • Implement smoke tests for quick deployment validation

Performance and Load Testing

  • Integrate performance testing into your pipeline
  • Use tools like k6, JMeter, or Artillery for load testing
  • Establish performance baselines and fail builds that regress
  • Monitor application performance metrics continuously

4. Optimize Pipeline Performance and Reliability

Fast feedback loops are essential for developer productivity. Optimizing pipeline performance while maintaining reliability is a critical balance.

Performance Optimization Strategies:

  • Run independent stages in parallel to reduce total execution time
  • Use build matrices for testing across multiple environments
  • Implement intelligent test selection based on code changes
  • Cache dependencies and build artifacts effectively
  • Cache package dependencies (npm, Maven, pip packages)
  • Use Docker layer caching for container builds
  • Implement build artifact caching across pipeline runs
  • Consider distributed caching solutions for large-scale operations
  • Order pipeline stages from fastest to slowest
  • Implement early exit strategies for critical failures
  • Use quality gates to prevent flawed code from progressing
  • Provide clear, actionable failure messages

5. Establish Robust Monitoring and Observability

Modern CI/CD pipelines require comprehensive monitoring to ensure reliability and quick issue resolution.

Observability Best Practices:

  • Track build success rates, duration, and failure patterns
  • Monitor deployment frequency and lead time for changes
  • Measure mean time to recovery (MTTR) for failed deployments
  • Implement alerting for pipeline anomalies
  • Integrate application performance monitoring (APM) tools
  • Implement structured logging throughout your applications
  • Use distributed tracing for microservices architectures
  • Set up real-time alerting for critical application metrics

Infrastructure Monitoring

  • Monitor resource utilization of your CI/CD infrastructure
  • Track container and Kubernetes cluster health
  • Implement cost monitoring for cloud resources
  • Use infrastructure monitoring tools like Prometheus, Grafana, or DataDog

6. Implement Progressive Deployment Strategies

Modern deployment strategies reduce risk and enable rapid rollback when issues arise.

Advanced Deployment Patterns:

  • Maintain two identical production environments
  • Switch traffic between environments for zero-downtime deployments
  • Enable instant rollback capabilities
  • Reduce deployment risk through environment isolation
  • Gradually roll out changes to a subset of users
  • Monitor key metrics during canary deployment
  • Implement automatic rollback triggers based on metrics
  • Use feature flags to control feature exposure
  • Update instances gradually while maintaining service availability
  • Implement health checks to ensure successful updates
  • Configure proper readiness and liveness probes
  • Plan for stateful application updates

7. Foster Team Collaboration and Culture

Technical excellence must be paired with strong team practices and culture.

  • Make build failures everyone’s responsibility
  • Implement “you build it, you run it” principles
  • Encourage cross-functional collaboration
  • Share knowledge through documentation and code reviews
  • Conduct regular retrospectives on pipeline performance
  • Experiment with new tools and practices
  • Measure and optimize developer experience
  • Maintain comprehensive pipeline documentation

Commit Frequently, Integrate Early

  • Encourage small, frequent commits
  • Implement trunk-based development where appropriate
  • Minimize long-lived feature branches
  • Ensure all changes go through the same quality gates

8. Plan for Disaster Recovery and Business Continuity

Modern CI/CD pipelines must be resilient and recoverable.

Disaster Recovery Strategies:

  • Regularly backup pipeline configurations and data
  • Test recovery procedures periodically
  • Implement cross-region redundancy for critical systems
  • Document recovery procedures clearly
  • Design pipelines for multi-region deployment capabilities
  • Implement proper data synchronization strategies
  • Plan for region failover scenarios
  • Test disaster recovery procedures regularly

Tools and Technologies for 2025

The CI/CD tooling landscape continues to evolve. Here are some trending technologies and tools to consider:

  • GitHub Actions (excellent GitHub integration)
  • GitLab CI/CD (comprehensive DevOps platform)
  • Jenkins (flexible, plugin-rich)
  • CircleCI (cloud-native focus)
  • Azure DevOps (Microsoft ecosystem integration)
  • AWS CodePipeline (AWS-native solution)
  • AI-powered pipeline optimization tools
  • Kubernetes-native CI/CD solutions (Tekton, Argo Workflows)
  • GitOps platforms (ArgoCD, Flux)
  • Advanced security scanning tools
  • Infrastructure automation platforms (Spacelift, Env0)

Node.js Specific Considerations

For Node.js applications, consider these additional best practices:

  • Use npm audit or yarn audit for vulnerability scanning
  • Implement proper package-lock.json management
  • Consider using npm ci for deterministic builds
  • Regularly update dependencies and monitor for security issues
  • Use multi-stage Docker builds to reduce image size
  • Implement proper .dockerignore files
  • Consider using Alpine-based images for smaller footprint
  • Optimize bundle sizes for web applications
  • Use Jest or Mocha for unit testing
  • Implement API testing with tools like Supertest
  • Use ESLint and Prettier for code quality
  • Consider TypeScript for large applications

Building effective CI/CD pipelines in 2025 requires a holistic approach that balances speed, security, reliability, and maintainability. By implementing these best practices, organizations can create resilient delivery mechanisms that support rapid innovation while maintaining high quality standards.

The key to success lies in starting with strong foundations — security, testing, and monitoring — then continuously iterating and improving based on feedback and metrics. Remember that the best CI/CD pipeline is one that enables your team to deliver value to customers quickly and confidently.

As we continue through 2025, staying current with emerging trends like AI-driven automation, advanced security practices, and cloud-native technologies will be crucial for maintaining competitive advantage in software delivery.

What are your experiences with modern CI/CD practices? Share your thoughts and challenges in the comments below. If you found this guide helpful, please give it a clap and follow for more insights on modern software development practices.

In the standard Kubernetes model, a node’s suitability for workloads hinges on a single binary "Ready" condition. However, in modern Kubernetes environments, nodes require complex infrastructure dependencies—such as network agents, storage drivers, GPU firmware, or custom health checks—to be fully operational before they can reliably host pods.

Today, on behalf of the Kubernetes project, I am announcing the Node Readiness Controller. This project introduces a declarative system for managing node taints, extending the readiness guardrails during node bootstrapping beyond standard conditions. By dynamically managing taints based on custom health signals, the controller ensures that workloads are only placed on nodes that met all infrastructure-specific requirements.

Why the Node Readiness Controller?

Core Kubernetes Node "Ready" status is often insufficient for clusters with sophisticated bootstrapping requirements. Operators frequently struggle to ensure that specific DaemonSets or local services are healthy before a node enters the scheduling pool.

The Node Readiness Controller fills this gap by allowing operators to define custom scheduling gates tailored to specific node groups. This enables you to enforce distinct readiness requirements across heterogeneous clusters, ensuring for example, that GPU equipped nodes only accept pods once specialized drivers are verified, while general purpose nodes follow a standard path.

It provides three primary advantages:

  • Custom Readiness Definitions: Define what means for your specific platform.
  • Automated Taint Management: The controller automatically applies or removes node taints based on condition status, preventing pods from landing on unready infrastructure.
  • Declarative Node Bootstrapping: Manage multi-step node initialization reliably, with a clear observability into the bootstrapping process.

Core concepts and features

The controller centers around the NodeReadinessRule (NRR) API, which allows you to define declarative for your nodes.

Flexible enforcement modes

The controller supports two distinct operational modes:

Actively maintains the readiness guarantee throughout the node’s entire lifecycle. If a critical dependency (like a device driver) fails later, the node is immediately tainted to prevent new scheduling.
Specifically for one-time initialization steps, such as pre-pulling heavy images or hardware provisioning. Once conditions are met, the controller marks the bootstrap as complete and stops monitoring that specific rule for the node.

The controller reacts to Node Conditions rather than performing health checks itself. This decoupled design allows it to integrate seamlessly with other tools existing in the ecosystem as well as custom solutions:

  • Readiness Condition Reporter: A lightweight agent provided by the project that can be deployed to periodically check local HTTP endpoints and patch node conditions accordingly.

Operational safety with dry run

Deploying new readiness rules across a fleet carries inherent risk. To mitigate this, mode allows operators to first simulate impact on the cluster. In this mode, the controller logs intended actions and updates the rule's status to show affected nodes without applying actual taints, enabling safe validation before enforcement.

Example: CNI bootstrapping

The following NodeReadinessRule ensures a node remains unschedulable until its CNI agent is functional. The controller monitors a custom cniplugin.example.net/NetworkReady condition and only removes the readiness.k8s.io/acme.com/network-unavailable taint once the status is True.

items.title: AWS Weekly Roundup: Amazon Bedrock agent workflows, Amazon SageMaker private connectivity, and more (February 2, 2026)
items.author: Betty Zheng (郑予彬)
items.content:
Over the past week, we passed Laba festival, a traditional marker in the Chinese calendar that signals the final stretch leading up to the Lunar New Year. For many in China, it’s a moment associated with reflection and preparation, wrapping up what the year has carried, and turning attention toward what lies ahead.

Looking forward, next week also brings Lichun, the beginning of spring and the first of the 24 solar terms. In Chinese tradition, spring is often seen as the season when growth begins and new cycles take shape. There’s a common saying that “a year’s plans begin in spring,” capturing the idea that this is a time to set one’s direction and start fresh.

Here are the launches that got my attention this week:

  • Amazon Bedrock enhances support for agent workflows with server-side tools and extended prompt caching – Amazon Bedrock introduced two updates that improve how developers build and operate AI agents. The Responses API now supports server-side tool use, so agents can perform actions such as web search, code execution, and database updates within AWS security boundaries. Bedrock also adds a 1-hour time-to-live (TTL) option for prompt caching, which helps improve performance and reduce the cost for long-running, multi-turn agent workflows. Server-side tools are available with OpenAI GPT OSS 20B and 120B models, and the 1-hour prompt caching TTL is generally available for select Claude models by Anthropic in Amazon Bedrock.
  • Amazon S3 adds support for changing object encryption without data movement – Amazon S3 now supports changing the server-side encryption type of existing encrypted objects without moving or re-uploading data. Using the API, you can switch from SSE-S3 to SSE-KMS, rotate customer -managed AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys, or standardize encryption across buckets at scale with S3 Batch Operations while preserving object properties and lifecycle eligibility.
  • Amazon Keyspaces introduces table pre-warming for predictable high-throughput workloads – Amazon Keyspaces (for Apache Cassandra) now supports table pre-warming, which helps you proactively set warm throughput levels so tables can handle high read and write traffic instantly without cold-start delays. Pre-warming helps reduce throttling during sudden traffic spikes, such as product launches or sales events, and works with both on-demand and provisioned capacity modes, including multi-Region tables. The feature supports consistent, low-latency performance while giving you more control over throughput readiness.

Here are some additional projects, blog posts, and news items that I found interesting:

  • Amazon EventBridge increases event payload size to 1 MB – Amazon EventBridge now supports event payloads up to 1 MB, an increase from the previous 256 KB limit. This update helps event-driven architectures carry richer context in a single event, including complex JSON structures, telemetry data, and machine learning (ML) or generative AI outputs, without splitting payloads or relying on external storage.
  • AWS MCP Server adds deployment agent SOPs (preview) – AWS introduced deployment standard operating procedures (SOPs) that AI agents can deploy web applications to AWS from a single natural language prompt in MCP -compatible integrated development environments (IDEs) and command line interfaces (CLIs) such as Kiro, Cursor, and Claude Code. The agent generates AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) infrastructure, deploys AWS CloudFormation stacks, and sets up continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) workflows following AWS best practices. The preview supports frameworks including React, Vue.js, Angular, and Next.js.
  • AWS Lambda adds enhanced observability for Kafka event source mappings – AWS Lambda introduced enhanced observability for Kafka event source mappings, providing Amazon CloudWatch Logs and metrics to monitor event polling configuration, scaling behavior, and event processing state. The update improves visibility into Kafka-based Lambda workloads, helping teams diagnose configuration issues, permission errors, and function failures more efficiently. The capability supports both Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK) and self-managed Apache Kafka event sources.
  • AWS CloudFormation 2025 year in review – This year-in-review post highlights CloudFormation updates delivered throughout 2025, with a focus on early validation, safer deployments, and improved developer workflows. It covers enhancements such as improved troubleshooting, drift-aware change sets, stack refactoring, StackSets updates, and new -IDE and AI -assisted tooling, including the CloudFormation language server and the Infrastructure as Code (IaC) MCP server.

Check your calendars so that you can sign up for this upcoming event:

AWS Community Day Romania (April 23–24, 2026) – This community-led AWS event brings together developers, architects, entrepreneurs, and students for more than 10 professional sessions delivered by AWS Heroes, Solutions Architects, and industry experts. Attendees can expect expert-led technical talks, insights from speakers with global conference experience, and opportunities to connect during dedicated networking breaks, all hosted at a premium venue designed to support collaboration and community engagement.

If you’re looking for more ways to stay connected beyond this event, join the AWS Builder Center to learn, build, and connect with builders in the AWS community.

items.title: ColdFusion AWS S3 Bucket Access Denied: A Complete Troubleshooting Guide
items.author: Deepak Purohit
items.content:
Unlocking Access: Solving AWS S3 “Access Denied” Errors in ColdFusion

Integrating AWS S3 with ColdFusion is a powerful combination. It provides scalable, durable cloud storage for your applications. However, an “Access Denied” error stops this integration abruptly. Your application cannot read or write files. This frustrating error is a common gatekeeper. It signals a breakdown in the complex AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) system. The good news is this error is highly solvable. Permission issues follow logical patterns. This guide provides a systematic diagnostic path. You will learn to inspect IAM policies and bucket settings. We will also cover ColdFusion configuration details. Your application will soon communicate with S3 seamlessly. Let’s unlock your bucket access together.

Understanding the AWS S3 Access Model

AWS secures resources through layered permissions. An “Access Denied” error means a permission check failed. This failure can happen at several distinct levels. The request might be missing authentication credentials. The credentials might lack the necessary permissions. The bucket policy might explicitly deny the request. Even a VPC endpoint or object ownership could be the culprit. Diagnosing the exact layer is your first crucial task. We will examine each layer methodically.

Layer 1: ColdFusion AWS Credentials Configuration

ColdFusion needs valid AWS credentials to make requests. These are typically an Access Key ID and Secret Access Key. They must be stored securely in your ColdFusion application. The most common method uses the cfusion S3 extension settings.

Verifying Credentials in the ColdFusion Administrator

Navigate to the ColdFusion Administrator. Go to “Extensions” > “Amazon S3”. Ensure your S3 connection is configured. Check the “Access Key ID” and “Secret Access Key” fields. Are they correct and current? AWS IAM credentials can be deactivated or rotated. Verify the key’s status in the AWS IAM console. The key must be “Active”. Also, ensure no extra spaces surround the key values. A stray character invalidates the credential.

Using IAM User Credentials (Not Root Keys)

Never use your AWS root account credentials. Create a dedicated IAM user for ColdFusion. Grant this user only the permissions it needs. This follows the principle of least privilege. It also improves security and auditability. The “Access Denied” error may indicate insufficient user permissions. We will fix this in the IAM policy layer next.

Layer 2: IAM User Policies and Permissions

The IAM user needs an attached policy. This policy defines what S3 actions are allowed. An incomplete policy causes “Access Denied” errors.

Minimum S3 Policy for Basic Operations

Create a custom IAM policy in the AWS console. Attach it to your ColdFusion IAM user. Below is a policy for common read/write operations.

{    "Version": "2012-10-17",        {            "Action": [                "s3:GetObject",                "s3:DeleteObject",            ],                "arn:aws:s3:::YOUR-BUCKET-NAME",
                "arn:aws:s3:::YOUR-BUCKET-NAME/*"
            ]    ]

Notice the two Resource lines. The first line (arn:aws:s3:::BUCKET) allows bucket-level actions like ListBucket. The second line (arn:aws:s3:::BUCKET/*) allows object-level actions like GetObject. Missing the wildcard (/*) is a classic mistake. It leads to confusing "Access Denied" for object operations. Update your IAM user's policy accordingly. Replace YOUR-BUCKET-NAME with your actual bucket name.

Layer 3: S3 Bucket Policy Configuration

The bucket itself has a resource-based policy. This policy can override IAM user permissions. A misconfigured bucket policy can deny all access. View your bucket policy in the AWS S3 console. Select your bucket, then go to “Permissions” > “Bucket Policy”.

Example Bucket Policy Granting User Access

A bucket policy can grant your IAM user specific permissions. Use the IAM user’s unique ARN (Amazon Resource Name).

{    "Version": "2012-10-17",        {
            "Sid": "AllowColdFusionUser",
            "Effect": "Allow",                "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::YOUR-ACCOUNT-ID:user/YOUR-IAM-USERNAME"            "Action": [                "s3:PutObject",            ],
            "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::YOUR-BUCKET-NAME/*"
        }}

Find your IAM user’s ARN in the IAM console. Insert it into the Principal field. Ensure the bucket policy does not have an explicit "Effect": "Deny" rule. Such a rule would block your IAM user's request completely.

Layer 4: S3 Bucket Block Public Access Settings

AWS enables “Block Public Access” by default. This is a critical security feature. However, it can block legitimate private access in certain configurations. Review your bucket’s “Block Public Access” settings. Go to S3 console > Bucket > Permissions. Scroll to “Block Public Access”. If all four blocks are enabled, your bucket is private. This is usually correct for application access. However, check for any “Deny” effects in other policies. They might conflict with IAM allowances. The default “Block” settings should not affect IAM-authenticated requests. They primarily block anonymous public access.

Layer 5: Object Ownership and ACLs (S3 Object Ownership)

AWS introduced a new “Bucket owner enforced” setting. This simplifies permissions but can cause issues. Check your bucket’s “Object Ownership” setting. Go to S3 console > Bucket > Permissions. Find the “Object Ownership” section. There are two main settings: “ACLs disabled (recommended)” and “ACLs enabled”. For simplicity, choose “Bucket owner enforced” (ACLs disabled). This ensures the bucket owner owns all objects. It also ignores any legacy object ACLs. If “ACLs enabled” is selected, object-level ACLs might deny access. Align your object ownership with your access pattern. The experts at Lucid Outsourcing Solutions standardize on “Bucket owner enforced”. This avoids cryptic permission conflicts for their clients.

Layer 6: VPC Endpoints and Network Policies

Your ColdFusion server might be in an AWS VPC. Network access to S3 might require a VPC Endpoint. A missing or misconfigured endpoint causes access failure. Create a Gateway-type VPC Endpoint for S3. Ensure its policy allows access to your target bucket. Also, check security group and network ACL rules. They must allow outbound HTTPS (port 443) traffic. Without this, requests cannot even reach S3. The error might manifest as a network timeout. However, it can sometimes appear as a generic “Access Denied”.

Layer 7: ColdFusion Code and SDK Configuration

Your CFML code might have subtle bugs. Incorrect region specification is a common error. The S3 bucket region and client region must match.

Using the CFML S3 Extension Correctly

The cfusion S3 tag requires proper initialization. Ensure the region attribute matches your bucket's region.

<s3 action="listBucket" bucket="my-bucket" accessKeyId="#application.awsKey#" secretAccessKey="#application.awsSecret#" region="us-east-1">

Find your bucket’s region in the S3 console. It is listed next to the bucket name. A mismatch causes a redirect error. This error often appears as “Access Denied”. Always specify the region explicitly.

Using the AWS Java SDK within ColdFusion

You might use the AWS Java SDK via cfobject. The credentials provider chain must be configured. Here is a robust code example.

<cfscript>    // Load AWS SDK classes
    s3Client = createObject("java", "software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.S3Client").builder()
        .region(createObject("java", "software.amazon.awssdk.regions.Region").of("us-east-1"))            createObject("java", "software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.StaticCredentialsProvider").create(
                createObject("java", "software.amazon.awssdk.auth.credentials.AwsBasicCredentials").create(
                    application.awsKey,                )        )    // Perform an operation
    listRequest = createObject("java", "software.amazon.awssdk.services.s3.model.ListObjectsRequest").builder()
        .bucket("my-bucket")    response = s3Client.listObjects(listRequest);

This gives you fine-grained control. It also produces clearer error messages sometimes.

Systematic Diagnostic Checklist

Follow this ordered list to identify the problem.

  1. Credentials: Are the AWS Access Key and Secret Key valid and active?
  2. IAM Policy: Does the IAM user have a policy allowing the specific S3 action? Check the Action and Resource ARNs.
  3. Bucket Policy: Does the bucket policy deny the request? Or does it fail to allow your user’s ARN?
  4. Object Ownership: Is the bucket using “Bucket owner enforced”? If not, check object ACLs.
  5. Region: Does the ColdFusion client region match the S3 bucket region exactly?
  6. Request Signature: Are you using the correct AWS Signature Version 4? The modern SDKs handle this.
  7. Network: Can your ColdFusion server reach the S3 endpoint (s3.amazonaws.com)?
  8. Resource ARN: Is your resource ARN correctly formatted with the wildcard (/*) for objects?

Enabling AWS CloudTrail for Detailed Logging

CloudTrail logs all API calls to your AWS account. Enable it in the AWS Management Console. Go to CloudTrail and create a trail. Logs will be delivered to an S3 bucket. When an “Access Denied” occurs, check the CloudTrail logs. Look for the event with an errorCode of AccessDenied. The log includes the user, resource, and denied action. This is the definitive source of truth. It shows exactly which permission check failed. This evidence is invaluable for complex policies.

Testing with the AWS CLI for Isolation

Isolate ColdFusion from the equation. Test the IAM user’s permissions directly. Install the AWS Command Line Interface (CLI). Configure it with the same credentials.

aws configure# Enter the Access Key, Secret Key, and region.
aws s3 ls s3://your-bucket-name/

If this fails, the problem is in AWS, not ColdFusion. The CLI will provide a clearer AWS error message. Fix the IAM or bucket policy based on this feedback. Then retry your ColdFusion application.

Conclusion: A Methodical Approach to Permissions

AWS S3 “Access Denied” errors are permission puzzles. Solve them by examining each security layer sequentially. Start with the ColdFusion credential configuration. Validate the IAM user’s policy for correct actions and resource ARNs. Inspect the S3 bucket policy for explicit denies or missing allows. Verify the bucket’s Object Ownership setting. Ensure your client region matches the bucket region. Use diagnostic tools like CloudTrail and the AWS CLI. This systematic approach will reveal the exact blockage. Once corrected, your ColdFusion application will interact with S3 smoothly. You will leverage scalable cloud storage reliably. This integration unlocks powerful file management capabilities for your projects.

Are complex AWS permissions slowing down your development? Configuring secure, least-privilege access between ColdFusion and AWS services requires deep expertise. Their team specializes in architecting robust connections between ColdFusion applications and AWS, ensuring secure, efficient, and reliable operations. Let them handle the cloud complexity so you can focus on innovation.

items.title: How to Port Forward Traffic to a Remote IP Using Iptables
items.author: Mobin Shaterian
items.content:
In the world of networking, you often find yourself in a situation where a vital service — like a Swagger API dashboard — is hosted on a server that isn’t directly reachable by everyone on your team. Whether due to subnet isolation, VPN restrictions, or firewall policies, these “network silos” can stall development and testing.

This article provides a step-by-step technical walkthrough on how to use to turn a standard Linux machine into a transparent bridge. By leveraging Destination NAT (DNAT) and Source NAT (SNAT), you can map a local port on your gateway machine to a remote service, effectively “proxying” the connection at the kernel level for maximum performance and reliability.

  • ip_target:4000 (The "hidden" service you can access) like 10.100.100.10:400
  • ip_gateway (Your machine's IP on the network).
  • 9099 (The port users will use to reach the service).

Step 1: Enable Kernel-Level Forwarding

By default, most Linux distributions disable the ability to pass traffic between different network interfaces for security reasons. You must tell the kernel to behave like a router.

cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward

sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
Note: To make this permanent after a reboot, edit /etc/sysctl.conf and uncomment the line net.ipv4.ip_forward=1.

Step 2: Destination NAT (PREROUTING)

The PREROUTING chain in the handles packets as they first hit your network card. Here, we change the "envelope" of the packet: we swap your IP address for the target service's IP address.

sudo iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 9099 -j DNAT --to-destination ip_target:4000

Any TCP traffic hitting your machine on port 9099 is immediately redirected to ip_target on port 4000.

Step 3: Open the Firewall (FORWARD)

Even if the packet is redirected, the Linux firewall (Filter table) will drop it by default if your policy is set to DROP. You must explicitly grant permission for these packets to cross through your system.

# 1. Allow established connections back insudo iptables -I FORWARD 1 -m state --state RELATED,ESTABLISHED -j ACCEPT
# 2. Allow new requests to the target destinationsudo iptables -I FORWARD 2 -p tcp -d ip_gateway --dport 4000 -j ACCEPT

Step 4: Source NAT (POSTROUTING)

This is the most critical and often forgotten step. When the target service (ip_target) receives a packet, it needs to know where to send the reply.

If we don’t use , the service will try to reply directly to the original user’s IP. Since the user never asked ip_target for anything (they asked ), their computer will reject the reply.

sudo iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -p tcp -d ip_target --dport 4000 -j MASQUERADE

It “masks” the original user’s IP with your own gateway IP. The target service replies to you, and you safely pass that reply back to the user.

Step 5: Verification and Testing

To verify the rules are active, list the NAT table with line numbers and packet counters:

sudo iptables -t nat -L -n -v --line-numbers
  • While testing, run sudo iptables -t nat -L -n -v. If the pkts (packets) column increases, your traffic is successfully hitting the rule.

Mastering for port forwarding is more than just running a single command; it is about understanding how packets flow through the Linux networking stack. By correctly configuring the , , and chains, you have successfully built a transparent bridge that bypasses network isolation without the overhead of a traditional proxy server.

  • Forwarding requires three distinct actions: translating the destination (DNAT), permitting the pass-through (FORWARD), and masking the source for the return trip (MASQUERADE).
  • No amount of iptables rules will work if the kernel’s ip_forward setting is disabled.
  • Using the -v (verbose) flag to monitor packet counters is the most effective way to debug where a connection is being dropped.

With this setup, your gateway machine now provides a seamless entry point for your team, making the “hidden” Swagger UI at ip_target as accessible as any local resource. Just remember to save your rules using iptables-persistent to ensure your bridge survives the next system reboot.

items.title: How to Make the Ops and DevOps Work Better and Faster with AI
items.author: Peter Gillich
items.content:
This article describes a way, how AI can operate on Kubernetes clusters by GitOps and direct way, with human control.

If you cannot see the whole article, click .

Problem: Traditional Documentation doesn’t Work

I’m working in a team, which provides observability services on Kubernetes clusters. Most of the work is DevOps, Ops, but sometime development in Python or Golang. The 24/7 standby is handled by an another support team. The deployment and configuration is managed with Application Controller (ArgoCD) by GitOps way.

My team is responsible for everything from setup a new Kubernetes cluster with all services, trough handling user requests, until incident handling in worktime. Out of the worktime, the incidents are handled by another 24/7 support team.

Wide competence, experience and willingness to self-learning are required to this job. The learning curve takes long time, but honestly, it takes forever. From knowledge point of view, the most critical is the 24/7 support team member, who don’t have time and chance to get enough competence and experience to make responsible operation on our Kubernetes cluster.

Several knowledge sharing page were made, but it aren’t useful for incidents: each of them is different story and we cannot write enough detailed and well structured Runbooks for anybody.

Our system is not enough robust, because of a tradeoff. The FinOps organization pushes the my team to use as less as possible resources to keep the operational cost low. Our users want to have 99.9% availability, which needs more idle resources, which is more expensive.

So, The allocated base resource consumption is 2–3 times higher than the average real usage, in order to handle small usage peaks. If the usage (CPU or RAM) is higher, autoscaler will start a new instance or node. But this autoscaling does not work perfectly in each cases on our heterogeneous system. Most of the incidents in the last year were resource usage issues: not enough resource (CPU, RAM, storage) or limits (message size, messages/sec, MB/s).

Goal: AI as a Tool to Glue Everything

The traditional info sharing could not be enough good in the team, so we have make a paradigm change.

Instead of trying to figure out all the possible incident cases (which is not possible) and trying to write documentation for anybody (which is also not possible), we decided to follow another approach: promote the AI as the main tool for configuring, troubleshooting and incident handling.

The AI will be the glue between several information and will collect the information from live systems automatically. Based on this information, AI will provide solution alternatives with executable commands on live systems or pull requests to GitOps repos.

There are several roles, who has different competence, experience and expectation:

These engineers must know several systems, so they are not able to know each system enough deeply. They will work on our Kubernetes clusters out of the worktime and their goal is hotfix or workaround our system until worktime, when my team will handover the incident and will make the final solution.

Most of the incidents are related to resource consumption or reaching a rate limit, so they should be able to identify it and add more resource and/or increase a limit. These changes may be made with GitOps or without GitOps (directly on the live system) operation.

The AI should discover the cluster, identify the bottleneck and should provide solution alternatives and commands which should be executed on the cluster by one click or should be a pull request to GitOps.

Any job grade (intern, junior, medior, senior, staff, etc.) can have this role, mostly the newcomers in the team. They have access to all the clusters (including test, sandbox) git repos, documentations. But they don’t have experience on our system, they don’t know how our system can be discovered, they don’t know where can be found the proper config files.

They should be able to implement tickets alone as soon as possible. They can access our test and sandbox clusters, so they can independently try out solution alternatives that they are unsure of.

The AI should help them similar to 24/7 Support Engineer, but their preference is different: they should prefer the long-term GitOps solution, instead of the direct change on live system. The preference depends on the task: if the task is an incident handling, the direct change of the system is acceptable (until the final solution has not deployed by GitOps).

AI does not know the different preference, depending on the task type, so the engineers must be prepared for selecting the solution alternatives, depending on the case.

Higher job grade (medior, senior, staff, etc.) can have this role. This role integrates a new solution, service, application or implements a new feature in Python or Golang.

These engineers must read several internal and external documentation. The engineer may be in contact to users or Product Owners. The new features should be tested on the test or sandbox cluster, before deploying it to live clusters.

The AI should help them similar to Junior Team Members and should support them to learn new things. Most of the time this role does not work on the live nodes.

Concerns: Responsibility and Information

AI is a buzzword in IT world nowadays. In DevOps and Ops domain, AI is mostly used only to get useful information. Operating by AI on a live system is risky, so human control is suggested, without human control it’s science fiction. Typical issues and concerns with using AI in Ops and DevOps domain:

  • Responsibility: Who will be the responsible, if AI suggests a bad solution or makes a mistake on a live system?
  • Unpredictable behavior: The base concept of LLMs is figuring out the next words and sentences, based on the the learned info and using probability. The result of the conceptual probability, the result will be different sometime.
  • Lack of information: AI does not join to informal conversations, where the key principles and concepts are decided and shared verbal.
  • Custom information: The team way of working and priorities of solution alternatives are different to the AI-known typical methods.
  • Quality of information: A part of shared information on the corporate intranet is not maintained and will be obsoleted.
  • Heterogeneous information: The needed information to make good decision on live systems are in different format, which may not be understable by AI
  • Fragmented information: The needed information is at several places
  • No access to information: The information on corporate intranet can be accessed by different way and credentials.

Based on above, the engineer is the responsible. The AI is only a tool, which can present what it discovered and can suggest solution alternatives. The engineer has to make sure, any change on live system and in the GitOps is safe.

So, the AI can only help the engineer’s work, who will make better solution faster.

Solution: VSCode + Copilot

My company took a smart decision: use only GitHub Enterprise for version control and GitOps. If company needs a service and it exists on GitHub, it will be selected, instead of another competitors. An example for it is the Copilot for AI.

VSCode is using in my team with Copilot Chat. In the past, Copilot was using in Ask mode with ChatGPT mode, because it was the default. After a while, we changed to Agent mode and Anthropic Clause model, mostly the Sonnet. This setup is enough for feature and deployment implementing.

AGENTS.md for DevOps and Ops

There was an important decision: the solution must be used to real clusters from the beginning with strict control (on sandbox and test clusters first), in order to get enough experience and have safe context config for using this solution on live clusters.

When I tried to to use Copilot for DevOps and Ops activities, I had to set a lot of information for the context, which was annoying and obstructive. The solution was creating AGENTS.md files in each root of cluster repositories (*-infra, *-controller, *-helm), which are added automatically to the context by Copilot, if these repos are in the VSCode workspace. When I set the cluster name at the beginning of the promt, so Copilot can pick the selected cluster-related information from the AGENTS.md files.

The AGENTS.md files can be placed at another directory, for example .github/copilot-instructions.md , but it’s too specific for Copilot. It may be important, when we want to use Copilot Agent, running on the GitHub web page.

At the first time, I asked Copilot to write AGENTS.md files, based on what I wrote in the promt and what it discovered in the repos. The result were 500-lines-length files, which are added to the context automatically. These long files consume tokens of the limited token number, so it should be shorter. I used Writing a good CLAUDE.md suggestions to make them shorter (less is more: write only information, which cannot be discovered from the repo). To make AGENTS.md files more shorter, I put AGENTS.md file to obs-ai repo with cluster-independent information.

Below information is in the AGENTS.md files:

  • What this repo is used for.
  • Purpose and role description (what kind of engineers will use the promt).
  • Relationship between the repos of one cluster (*-infra, *-controller, *-helm).
  • Reference to another repos (local git directory, GitHub URL): private and public.
  • Kubectl connection info to the cluster (config file location, kubectl context).
  • Autoscaling, high availability and multizone concept
  • Notice the users of the cluster (tenants)
  • Notice the main services of the cluster (Grafana stack: Loki, Mimir, Tempo, Grafana UI)
  • Notice the main data flow of the cluster (telemetry endpoint and pipeline)
  • Notice about network setup (Istio)
  • Troubleshooting guidance and preferences
  • Troubleshooting info references: Runbooks

Generating initial AGENTS.md

I generated the initial AGENTS.md file by below promt:

Create AGENTS.md for each below repositories, which will be used by Copilot AI agents, especially Calaude Sonnet 4.5 . The developers will use Copilot chat to change and improve the cluster deployments. If needed, use kubectl commands to discover the cluster. The Copilot prompts should be able to use kubectl commands to discover and validate the current configuration.
Discover and describe which services are deployed in each repositories. Discover and describe how the deployments and services are related between the repositories. Make more detailed discovery for Grafana, Loki, Mimir, Tempo, Alloy, OpenTelemetry Gateway and Istio. Make more detailed discovery for the pattern of telemetry data path, managed by OTEL operator with opentelemetrycollectors.opentelemetry.io CR, but do not list each Tenant Applications and Tenant Namespaces, because it will be extended in the future. Make more detailed discovery for self monitoring and log collection (telemetry) in org-obs.
Discover and describe the referred Helm charts.
I have a Kubernetes cluster named cluster-1.
This cluster can be accessed by below kubectl configuration:
Kubectl config file: $HOME/.kube/cluster-1.yaml
Kubectl context: cluster-1
This cluster can be managed by below repositories:
Terraform deployment for infrastructure:
* Git URL: https://github.com/company-org-infra/cluster-1-infra
* Local directory: cluster-1
Terraform deployment for services:
* Git URL: https://github.com/company-org-obs/cluster-1-controller
* Local directory: cluster-1-config
* Git URL: https://github.com/company-org-obs/cluster-1-helm
* Local directory: cluster-1-cluster-resources
More info about referred charts:
* Helm repo URL: https://nexus.company.int/repository/obs-charts/
* Git URL: https://github.com/company-org-obs/obs-agent
* Local directory: obs-agent* Helm repo URL: https://nexus.company.int/repository/obs-charts/
* Git URL: https://github.com/company-org-obs/telemetry-gateway
* Local directory: telemetry-gateway* Helm repo URL: https://grafana.github.io/helm-charts/
* Git URL: https://github.com/grafana/helm-charts
* Local directory: ../github/grafana/helm-charts/charts/grafana* Helm repo URL: https://grafana.github.io/helm-charts/
* Git URL: https://github.com/grafana/loki
* Local directory: ../github/grafana/loki/production/helm/loki* Helm repo URL: https://grafana.github.io/helm-charts/
* Git URL: https://github.com/grafana/mimir
* Local directory: ../github/grafana/mimir/main/operations/helm
The parent directory to local repositories is $HOME/work/src, but it's different for the developers, so use relative directory references.
Validate yourself, do not hallucinate.

During the usage, I had to improve the AGENTS.md files, for example:

  • Versions: remove specified versions (it will be updated always).
  • Guidance: check Istio config in the repos and on the cluster, if communication errors.
  • Guidance: if pod not able to schedule, analyze the reason more deeply
  • Guidance: check if the Deployment/StatefulSet/Daemonset is managed by operator; if yes, change the CR
  • Infrastructure: adescription about 3-zone high-availability setup.
  • Safety: highlight (warn) if the kubectl command wants to change the cluster.
  • Optimization: do not use another cluster’s AGENTS.md file.

The harmful and harmless commands executed by Copilot Chat are defined in the VSCode workspace file, for example:

"settings": { "chat.tools.terminal.autoApprove": {  "/kubectl.*\\b(annotate|apply|attach|auth|autoscale|certificate|cordon|cp|create|delete|drain|edit|exec|expose|kustomize|label|patch|replace|rollout|run|scale|set|taint|uncordon)\\b/": false,  "uniq": true,  "/^yq\\b.*(-[a-zA-Z]*i[a-zA-Z]*|--inplace)\\b/": false,  ...}

Confluence pages and Runbooks

I gave connection info to company Confluence pages for the Copilot Chat, in order to get additional troubleshooting information, but processing the HTML responses was not enough good. Instead, I made a simple Python code in the obs-ai repo by vibe coding to fetch the selected index pages and its references and convert it to Markdown files into docs/md directory. Copilot can process the Markdown files better.

The private and public Runbooks have similar issues, so it should be converted same way.

Tasks are managed by Jira in my team. The connection and info processing will be worked out in the future.

The Pod logs are stored in Grafana Loki. The connection way has not been worked out yet. Most probable, it will be fetched trough Grafana API, not directly from Loki API.

Temporary, Copilot Agent automatically runs the kubectl logs command can fetch the logs of running Pods, but not for stopped logs.

The metrics are stored in Grafana Mimir. The connection way has not been worked out yet. Most probable, it will be fetched trough Grafana API, not directly from Mimir API.

Temporary, Copilot Agent automatically runs the kubectl port-forward and curl command can fetch the metrics of running Pods, but not for a time range.

The alerts stored in Grafana Mimir. The connection way has not been worked out yet. Most probable, it will be fetched trough Grafana API, not directly from MimirAPI.

GitHub Copilot CLI is not in GA yet, so it’s disabled in my company. When it will be in GA, automation possibilities will be investigated. At the first, only typical info collection will be automated. Some automated change action may be possible, but not in the in the near future.

Below articles may be helpful:

My opinion about Copilot Agent for Ops and Devops is mixed. Most of time the executed commands for discovery are better than I should do, but a few time I could make better.

Sometime the issue analysis finds the root cause faster than me (or at least I find in the possible root cause in a list), but sometime It could not find it. So, additional hints must be added in a new promt command. It can be improved by extending the AGENTS.md files.

Most of the time, the right alternative in the provided solution alternatives list is not at the 1st place. The root cause of this inaccuracy can be:

  • Lack of information: the design and architecture decisions, WoWs are not written in AGENTS.md files (should be written there)
  • Use case: depending on the cluster delivery type (production, test, sandbox) and the engineer role, the best solution alternative can be different on same symptoms.

But overall, with competent human control, this AI solution is useful, safe and increases the team velocity and the service readiness SLOs.

Even though I wrote good documentation, it’s rarely found or read, so it’s not worth it. Sometimes even I don’t remember what and where I documented. It may be the cognitive limitation of heterogeneous DevOps and GitOps systems.

Using the AI assistant with well-configured context will be increase the confidence of the engineers. This human-controlled AI way promises better and more effective knowledge sharing and learning path.

The AI agent cannot take the best decision all the time, because of lack of information: the delivery type the engineer role and the non-documented info. The way of giving this information will increase the AI agent decision better and more safe in the future.

In of the Kubernetes Workshop Series, I focused on provisioning a production-grade Kubernetes cluster on Azure using and Infrastructure as Code (IaC) best practices. This session emphasized building scalable, secure, and repeatable Kubernetes infrastructure suitable for real-world production environments.

In Week 01 of the Kubernetes Workshop, we focused on building strong fundamentals by understanding , the shift from monolithic to microservices architecture, and the need for container orchestration. We also explored , core components, and essential objects that form the backbone of a Kubernetes cluster.

In , I’ll focus on building a production-grade Kubernetes cluster on Azure, fully provisioned using and Infrastructure as Code (IaC) best practices.

Pre requisites for Week 02

Before moving on to the Week 02 project, the following tools and platforms are required. Make sure these are set up and configured in your pc:

✔️ (Free tier is sufficient)✔️ ✔️ (Windows Subsystem for Linux)✔️ ✔️ & Terraform Version Manager✔️ & Terragrunt Version Manage✔️ (Kubernetes CLI)

Having these prerequisites in place ensures a smooth experience while building a production-level Kubernetes cluster on Azure using Terragrunt.

What is Terraform and Terragrunt

is an infrastructure as code tool that lets you define both cloud and on-prem resources in human-readable configuration files that you can version, reuse, and share. You can then use a consistent workflow to provision and manage all of your infrastructure throughout its lifecycle.

is a thin wrapper for that provides extra tools for keeping configurations DRY (Don’t Repeat Yourself), managing remote state, and orchestrating infrastructure across multiple environments. It enhances Terraform by enabling module inheritance, reducing code duplication, and simplifying complex tasks.

Step-by-step process of build K8’s cluster on Azure

Firstly, create a folder and named it as , then open this folder with in your pc. After open the CLI type below commands to switch that folder,

Then open this folder as VS code editor (code .).

Then login to as your Azure account. Type VS code terminal then insert your login credentials and after takes some time you can login to Azure CLI.

Go to the VS code editor create basically 3 files one by one such as , and

Open the file and added below content to it,

locals {  default_yaml_path     = find_in_parent_folders("empty.yaml")
  org                   = yamldecode(file(find_in_parent_folders("org.yaml")))
  subscription          = yamldecode(file(find_in_parent_folders("subscription.yaml")))
  resource_group        = yamldecode(file(find_in_parent_folders("resource_group.yaml")))
  environment           = yamldecode(file(find_in_parent_folders("environment.yaml", local.default_yaml_path)))
#Templatize the provider generator so it can be used for different providers
generate "provider" {
  path      = "provider.tf"
  if_exists = "overwrite_terragrunt"provider "azurerm" {  subscription_id = "${local.subscription.subscription_id}"EOF  backend = "azurerm"    path      = "backend.tf"  }    subscription_id      = local.subscription.state_subscription
    resource_group_name  = local.subscription.state_resource_group
    storage_account_name = local.subscription.state_storage_account
    container_name       = "terraform-state"
    key                  = "${path_relative_to_include()}/terraform.tfstate"}    local.org,    local.resource_group,)

Next open file and added below content,

org_name: Default Directory # Go to your azure account directories you can find your org name

Finally, open the file and add only to it. The reason for this is that if any file is not found or an error occurs, those details will be recorded in this file.

Next, we need to create a state lock in Azure. First, log in to your Azure account and create a resource group named  . Select your region and click the  button.

After that, create a storage account within this resource group. Search for in the Azure portal search bar and create a new storage account.

Select resource group as “”Insert a name to accountPreferred storage type: Azure Blob Storage or Azure Data Lake Storage Gen 2

Click the button to complete the creation process.

Next, open your storage account and create a container named

Once all Azure platform configurations are completed, return to and create a new folder named inside the folder. Then, check your current Azure subscription, copy its name, and create another folder with that subscription name inside the “” folder.

After that, create a file named “ inside the folder and add the following content to it.

state_subscription : <subscription_id>state_resource_group : <resource_group_name>

After all configurations are added both files and folders in the editor, the setup is complete. Next, we can verify whether the main configuration is provisioning correctly or not.

cd subscriptions/Azure\ for\ Students/resource-groups/terra-v2/resourcegroup/

    Create a Kubernetes cluster

    After that, we move on to creating a Kubernetes cluster on Azure. Before starting this process, we need to set up the cluster network, which includes creating .

    Create a new folder under the folder named , and inside it create another folder named . This folder contains all the configuration files required for creating the cluster network.

    After the cluster network is successfully provisioned, you can verify it in the as well. Now, the final step is to create a Kubernetes cluster using this network.

    Go back to and under the folder, create a new folder named . Inside this folder, create another folder named . This folder will contain all the configuration files required for creating the Kubernetes cluster.

    Under the folder, add two files named and .

    data "azurerm_virtual_network" "cluster_vnet" {  name                = "cluster-vnet-${var.resource_group_name}"
      resource_group_name = var.resource_group_name
    }
    data "azurerm_subnet" "cluster_subnet" {
      name                 = "cluster-subnet-${var.resource_group_name}"
      virtual_network_name = "cluster-vnet-${var.resource_group_name}"
      resource_group_name  = var.resource_group_name
    resource "azurerm_kubernetes_cluster" "k8s-ws-cluster" {  name                        = "k8s-ws-cluster-${var.resource_group_name}"
      resource_group_name         = var.resource_group_name
      location                    = var.location
      dns_prefix                  = var.resource_group_name
      kubernetes_version          = var.kubernetes_version
      #automatic_channel_upgrade = "patch"
      automatic_upgrade_channel   = "patch"
      image_cleaner_interval_hours = 48

        name                        = "system"
        node_count                  = 1
        vm_size                     = var.instance_type
        vnet_subnet_id              = data.azurerm_subnet.cluster_subnet.id
        temporary_name_for_rotation = "systemtemp"
        orchestrator_version        = var.kubernetes_version      drain_timeout_in_minutes      = 0
          max_surge                     = "10%"

    After that, open the terminal and navigate to the folder. Then run the command to provision the Kubernetes cluster.

    Once the process is complete, go to the and verify whether the cluster has been created successfully. Navigate to the resources section, where you will be able to see your Kubernetes cluster listed and running.

    Connect K8 cluster to local terminal

    Go to the Kubernetes cluster in the and click the option, which is located at the top of the cluster page. A panel will open on the right side displaying a set of commands.

    Copy the and execute it in the . Then, copy the , paste it into the terminal, and append --admin at the end of the command before executing it.

    Now, your Azure Kubernetes cluster is connected to your local terminal. You can start testing Kubernetes commands directly from this terminal. ( kubectl must be installed on your local machine.)

    First, check the kubectl version to verify that it is installed correctly and working as expected.

    Now, you can practice any Kubernetes commands directly from this terminal.

    kubectl get podskubectl apply -f pod.yaml

    Additionally, if you find this entire file and folder structure difficult to follow, you can refer to the GitHub repository below. It contains the complete project with all configurations used in this setup.

KodeKloud AWS Challenge — Day 34: Creating and Deploying a Python AWS Lambda Function Using AWS CLI

A hands-on walkthrough of building a simple Python-based Lambda function, packaging it correctly, and deploying it using AWS CLI — focusing on fundamentals every DevOps engineer must master.

Day 34 of the KodeKloud AWS Challenge continued the deep dive into , this time with a strong emphasis on hands-on execution using the AWS CLI.

Unlike console-heavy workflows, CLI-based Lambda creation mirrors , where infrastructure is scripted, repeatable, and version-controlled.

The goal was simple but intentional:

  • Write a Python Lambda function
  • Attach the correct IAM execution role

Simple task. Zero room for mistakes.

Task Overview (What Was Required)

  1. Create a Python Lambda handler file
  2. Zip the function correctly
  3. Create a Lambda function using AWS CLI
  4. Attach an existing IAM role
  5. Verify successful creation

All actions were performed from the using AWS CLI.

Concept Explanation: Why Lambda + CLI Matters

AWS Lambda removes the need to manage servers — but does not remove responsibility.

Using AWS CLI to deploy Lambda functions is critical because:

  • It integrates cleanly with CI/CD pipelines
  • It avoids click-ops drift
  • It enforces consistency across environments

In Amazon Web Services, serious teams deploy Lambda via CLI — not manual console clicks.

Step-by-Step Implementation (How It Was Done)

1️⃣ Created the Python Script

On the aws-client host, I created a file named:

  • Responds with HTTP-style output
  • Body: Welcome to KKE AWS Labs!

This confirms successful execution when invoked.

2️⃣ Zipped the Python Script

Lambda requires code to be uploaded as a ZIP archive.

  • Packaged the script into:
  • The Python file was at the
  • No nested directories (common mistake)

Incorrect zip structure is one of the top Lambda deployment failures.

3️⃣ Created the Lambda Function Using AWS CLI

Using AWS CLI on the aws-client host:

  • Lambda function name: xfusion-lambda-cli
  • Deployment package: function.zip
  • Execution role: lambda_execution_role

The CLI command uploaded the zip and created the function in one step.

This approach is scriptable, repeatable, and production-aligned.

4️⃣ Attached the IAM Execution Role

The function used the :

  • Role name: lambda_execution_role
  • Secure access without embedded credentials

No role = no execution.Wrong role = broken function.

5️⃣ Verified the Lambda Function

  • Function appeared in AWS Lambda console
  • Runtime and role were correctly set
  • No permission or deployment errors

At this point, the Lambda function was fully operational.

Architecture Overview (How Execution Works)

  • Lambda function is invoked
  • AWS assumes the attached IAM role
  • Temporary credentials are generated
  • Logs are written to CloudWatch

No servers.No keys.

  • Zipping the parent directory instead of the file
  • Incorrect runtime version
  • Missing or incorrect IAM role
  • Relying only on the console instead of CLI

If Lambda fails silently, start with IAM and package structure.

  • Lambda deployments should be CLI-driven
  • Packaging matters as much as code
  • IAM roles define Lambda capabilities
  • Serverless still requires discipline
  • Small functions teach big architectural lessons

Day 34 reinforced an important DevOps reality:

Serverless doesn’t remove complexity — it relocates it to permissions and packaging.

By creating and deploying a Lambda function using AWS CLI, this task aligned closely with how real teams automate serverless workloads in production.

This sets the foundation for:

  • Event-driven architectures
